stories.headline: Ohtani 'considerably' healthier, expected back in Dodgers' lineup Wednesday
stories.summary: Dodgers star Shohei Ohtani is "probably an eight or a nine" on a scale from 1 to 10, according to manager Dave Roberts, and is expected to return to the lineup Wednesday against the Padres.
stories.body:
LOS ANGELES -- Shohei Ohtani is expected to return to the lineup on Wednesday, the first day he is eligible to be activated off the injured list, and Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said he looks "considerably" healthier than he did a couple of weeks ago.

"If he was a five, he's probably an eight or a nine right now," Roberts said, referencing a 1-to-10 scale.

The Dodgers activated right-hander Roki Sasaki and center fielder Andy Pages off the IL on Tuesday, a major development in the leadup to October.

Sasaki, who has been recovering from a blister suffered in an Aug. 26 start, was available out of the bullpen for Tuesday's series opener against the San Diego Padres and could be an option to once again close out games in the postseason. Pages, who fractured his left hand on Aug. 22, will reprise his role as an everyday player at a premium position.

Ohtani landed on the IL because of lingering pain in his right biceps and left knee on Sept. 8 but began a hitting progression seven days ago and advanced to taking as many as 40 swings off Trajekt, the popular pitching simulator. Ohtani also ran the bases that day. On Tuesday, he went through his typical pregame workout.

Ohtani, 32, will only hit the rest of this season and was struggling in that realm before landing on the IL, compiling just seven hits and 22 strikeouts over his last 54 at-bats. Roberts previously indicated the plan is for Ohtani to play in all of the Dodgers' remaining five regular-season games to get re-acclimated to major league pitching.

Where he hits, though, is up for debate. In all likelihood, Ohtani will continue to lead off against opposing right-handed pitchers. But Mookie Betts' recent hot streak -- heading into this week, he was hitting.373/.468/.746 in September -- has Roberts weighing the possibility of batting him leadoff against lefties.

What Ohtani's return means for outfield prospect Josue De Paula is also an open question.

De Paula, 21, has eight hits and 10 walks in 38 plate appearances since temporarily replacing Ohtani at designated hitter. The Dodgers are strongly considering him as an option to be a left-handed bat off the bench during the postseason, though they might send him down as the corresponding move for activating Ohtani in order to give him at-bats in this week's Triple-A championship series.

The other candidate would be backup catcher Dalton Rushing, who has an elbow injury that is preventing him from throwing. Rushing is expected to be activated at some point in the next three days, but Roberts admitted it would be difficult for him to be thrust into a pinch-hitting role in October after playing in just four games since the start of September.

"There's potential slug with both those guys," Roberts said. "It's going to be a good debate."

stories.headline: Woman says she reported alleged 49ers impersonator to team in December
stories.summary: A woman who says she is a victim in the FBI's fraud case against Daejon Love said she sent a "complaint/concern" to the Niners in December 2025, eight months before Love was arrested and charged with wire fraud and conspiracy to commit wire fraud.
stories.body:
A woman who says she is a victim in the FBI's fraud case against Daejon Love, a man who is accused of impersonating a San Francisco 49ers player, told ESPN on Tuesday that she submitted a complaint about him via the team's website in December, eight months before he was arrested.

Gwen Herndon said she sent a "complaint/concern" form submission to the Niners on Dec. 20, 2025. According to her message, which was reviewed by ESPN, Herndon wrote that "there is a federal investigation surrounding a man pretending to be a 49ers player," naming Love, and saying he stole money from women and that "he is severely damaging the reputation of your team."

"I wanted you to be aware of the situation and hopefully proactive in denouncing his involvement on your team," she wrote in the message.

In the email exchange provided by Herndon, she received a response from a general Levi's Stadium guest services account a week later on Dec. 27, 2025.

"We take reports of individuals misrepresenting themselves as members of the San Francisco 49ers very seriously," the response said. "For safety and legal reasons, the team cannot comment on ongoing investigations or specific individuals. However, we appreciate you bringing this to our attention and encouraging proactive measures to protect the integrity of the organization.

"If you have information that could assist law enforcement or legal authorities, we encourage you to contact the appropriate agencies directly. Our internal team will also monitor any instances of impersonation and take action as appropriate to protect fans and the team's reputation. Thank you again for your vigilance and concern for the Niners community," the email said.

Herndon said she had no further contact with the 49ers after the email response in December. It's unclear whether anyone at the Niners reviewed the email Herndon said she sent. A Niners team source told ESPN last week that the team had not received any reports about Love before it was contacted by the FBI in August.

On Tuesday, a 49ers spokesperson declined to confirm the email's existence or to provide further comment on the email, citing the FBI's ongoing investigation.

Love and his alleged partner in the scheme, Taylor Chan, were arrested Aug. 24 and charged with wire fraud and conspiracy to commit wire fraud. Federal authorities said the duo defrauded more than two dozen women out of about $1.3 million.

Love would meet women via dating apps, falsely portray himself as a "legitimately wealthy" 49ers player or real estate investor and solicit money from them, the FBI said. According to federal court filings, Love was wearing 49ers apparel when he was arrested in Boise, Idaho, and "the FBI later learned from interviews that Love was in Boise as part of his scheme and was actively defrauding three more victims in Idaho."

The Portland (Oregon) FBI said last week its investigation began on Sept. 30, 2024. According to the FBI's criminal complaint, "Investigators interviewed representatives from both the NFL and the 49ers regarding [Love's] affiliation with the 49ers and NFL at large. The representatives confirmed [Love] has never been employed with the 49ers or the NFL."

In a news conference Friday, Portland FBI special agent in charge Doug Olson said the Niners were "completely cooperative" in the investigation.

"They were very helpful in doing things that most people think are probably pretty simple, but it's not always that easy to confirm," Olson said. "Like, this person was, like, never an employee, never a player, not even ever in the NFL. They were able to help with a lot of that stuff. They were completely cooperative throughout the entire investigation."

Herndon, 24, told ESPN that she contacted the Niners because she wanted to prevent Love from scamming anyone else.

"It was apparent to me that there were so many victims and there were going to continue to be victims unless a public statement was made and was very visible," she said. "I knew that based on how fast he was moving."

In a statement to ESPN, a spokesperson for the Portland FBI office said, "The FBI investigates alleged violations of federal crime, and those allegations have to be proven in court by prosecutors beyond a reasonable doubt. It's paramount that investigations are thorough and take the necessary time to build the case for prosecution. Some investigations, particularly white-collar investigations, can take years, and some may not lead to charges."

Olson said Friday that the agency had identified 35 more potential victims of Love since they arrested him in August.

Herndon said she reported her allegations of being scammed by Love to the FBI and to her local police department in Eugene, Oregon [Eugene police declined to release records on Love, citing an open case]. Herndon also created the Facebook group "Victims of Jon Love" as a way to warn others about Love. She also said she published an ad for four consecutive weeks in April 2025 in Eugene Weekly, the only way she could serve Love with a small claims' civil lawsuit, because she struggled to locate an address for him.

In March 2025, Herndon, a real estate agent, sued Love in small claims' civil court in Oregon, alleging that she gave Love $10,000 for an investment idea he pitched to her. She said that when she started asking questions about her investment and requested her money back, he blocked her.

Since then, Herndon says she has been trying to spread awareness about Love's fraud.

"Anyone I could try and get to listen to me," Herndon said. "There is not one avenue I did not take."

Herndon said she didn't respond to the email she received back from guest services because she was frustrated that another organization would not publicly denounce Love.

"I trusted the Niners and believed them in saying there wasn't much that they could do," she said. "It was enough for me to know that they knew. In their own right, I also think that they are a victim.

"It's unfortunate that it was possible that it [the email] wasn't escalated and seen the way I hoped it was."

stories.headline: 'I respect him as a player': Mason Cox quips Dayne Zorko ahead of Grand Final
stories.summary: Mason Cox and Dayne Zorko are set to reignite their rivalry in Saturday's Grand Final, meeting for the first time since their clash in last year's prelim in which Zorko ripped the big ruck's glasses off.
stories.body:
One of footy's more entertaining beefs is set to reignite in Saturday's AFL Grand Final, with Mason Cox and Dayne Zorko to meet on a footy field for the first time since last year's fiery preliminary final.

Playing for Collingwood in the 2025 preliminary final loss to the Lions, Cox kicked the opening goal of the game after Zorko was penalised for blocking Cox's run at the ball. The American nailed the set shot and ran at Zorko to rub it in.

The Brisbane veteran engaged with Cox, pulling the ruck's protective eyewear from him face in the fracas.

Zorko was fined $5000 for the act, and a war of words erupted in the aftermath.

Immediately after the game, the Lions star conceded he "probably" shouldn't have ripped Cox's glasses off.

"If a seven-foot guy comes running at you in the streets, what are you going to do? It doesn't really make sense to me that someone can initiate it, then you're just standing up for yourself and protecting yourself," he told SEN after the match. "Should I have grabbed his glasses? Probably not ... I don't really care, I get to play in a Grand Final this week."

Cox wasn't particularly complimentary of the Brisbane veteran in the days after the incident. Speaking on ESPN's Red Time podcast, Cox said he went after Zorko because it's easy to get in his head and he gave away the free kick that led to Cox's goal, but grabbing his prescribed eye protection was too far.

"I'll just say this, I think he's kind ... I think he's a great man, a great role model, a person I'd be great friends with ... are all things I would not say about Dayne Zorko," Cox said at the time.

Zorko missed the Round 12 clash between the Lions and Dockers earlier this year with a quad injury, meaning Saturday's Grand Final will be their first meeting on the footy field since that preliminary final.

When asked about the rivalry with Zorko on Red Time on Wednesday, Cox was full of praise for Zorko the player, but stopped short of quashing the beef with Zorko the man.

"I'd probably put my hand out and shake his hand," Cox said with a smile when asked what would happen if he kicked a goal and went looking for Zorko. "Look, Dayne's a great player, I know a lot of people love the jabs back and forth.

"He's a fantastic AFL player, there's no doubt about that, you've got to give the man credit where it's due. And yeah, look, he's obviously back in a Grand Final, three years straight.

"He's obviously the opposition this week, and you try to [do whatever you can do] to be able to get into other peoples' heads. I think myself and him are both firestarters, firecrackers -- whatever you want to call them -- for teams.

"So yeah, I respect him as a player."

Cox is aiming to win his second premiership after winning with Collingwood in 2023, while Zorko and the Lions are going for a threepeat, having won the 2024 and 2025 premierships.

stories.headline: 2026 NBA offseason trade grades: Finney-Smith, Schroder, more deals
stories.summary: We're grading the biggest NBA trades of the offseason, including the Atlanta deal that sent Hield and Nembhard to Charlotte for Finney-Smith.
stories.body:
The NBA offseason is here, with Aaron Wiggins' trade to the Atlanta Hawks on June 22 the first move in what has already been a frenzied offseason.

The big news came a day before the NBA draft, when Giannis Antetokounmpo was traded by the Milwaukee Bucks to the Miami Heat in a blockbuster. There was another big trade the morning after the draft, as the Charlotte Hornets shipped LaMelo Ball to the Minnesota Timberwolves. And the trades haven't stopped since.

I'm grading every trade this offseason, including draft deals, and breaking down the ramifications for all teams and players involved.

To determine each grade, I'm looking at multiple factors, including the on-court impact and ages of involved players, the cost in terms of draft picks and future financial implications, and the context of the team's short- and long-term outlooks. How risky or certain is the move? And how much does it help or hurt the team's chance to win the championship, next season or beyond?

Let's get into the latest moves:

Quick links:

Latest buzz | FA signing grades | Trade machine

Depth charts | Offseason guides | Draft coverage

Sept. 22: Hawks send Hield, Nembhard to Hornets for Finney-Smith

Charlotte Hornets get: G Buddy Hield, G Ryan Nembhard, cash considerations

Atlanta Hawks get: F Dorian Finney-Smith

Grade for Hawks: B+

For the Hawks, this swap of reserve wings is primarily about resolving a roster crunch, as they trade two players -- including backup guard Nembhard, whom they had initially acquired alongside Luguentz Dort in an earlier trade -- for one.

That fix comes at a minor price, as Finney-Smith will earn $14.2 million this season, compared with $11.8 million combined for Hield and Nembhard. (Finney-Smith and Hield are both nominally signed for additional years, but for zero guaranteed money.) The Hawks are reportedly sending cash to Charlotte in this deal, as well.

But this deal is smart business for the Hawks because it gives them another potential two-way contributor on the wing, as they build out a fearsome defensive rotation. Hield doesn't fit that mold, and he never seemed to find his footing in Atlanta. He arrived from Golden State in the Kristaps Porzingis trade last February but played just 51 minutes over the rest of the regular season, as the Hawks enjoyed their late-season surge without him.

Finney-Smith, meanwhile, was far worse than Hield last season, as he averaged only 3.3 points per game and made 27% of his 3s after returning from ankle surgery. That disappointing level of production incentivized Houston to trade him to Charlotte earlier this offseason, in a salary dump that brought the Hornets three second-round picks.

But as I wrote at the time of that initial trade, "Finney-Smith failed to launch in Houston, but he was a standout role player as recently as the 2024-25 season, due to his 3-and-D skill set and excellent on/off rating. Now 33 years old, Finney-Smith might just be done as an NBA rotation player, but he's also a reasonable bounce-back candidate from an injury-marred season, and could very well be a contributor in Charlotte."

Substitute "Atlanta" for "Charlotte" in that last sentence, and that analysis still holds for the Hawks.

Grade for Hornets: B-

If the Hornets didn't think Finney-Smith would bounce back for them, then at least they still gained three second-round picks for acquiring him, then saved some money by flipping him to Atlanta anyway.

Odds are that this trade won't move the needle much either way next season, but I would have preferred Charlotte to give Finney-Smith a shot to earn minutes. Hield has a track record of falling out of favor in several cities now, while Finney-Smith's reputation has suffered from just one bad year.

Still, the Hornets have a rather crowded rotation themselves, and Hield might fit Charlotte coach Charles Lee's preferred style better than he did Quin Snyder's in Atlanta. Charlotte led the NBA in 3-point makes and ranked third in 3-point percentage last season, and Hield is a career 39.5% shooter from distance.

Aug 19: Watson to Cavs, Strus to Clippers in multiteam deal

Cleveland Cavaliers get: G Peyton Watson, F Cam Whitmore

LA Clippers get: G Max Strus

Denver Nuggets get: F Julian Reese, unprotected first-round pick (2031, from CLE), second-round pick (2032, from SAC)

Washington Wizards get: G Tre Mann, second-round pick (2027, from CLE, via LAC), cash considerations

Grade for Cavaliers: B

Look at just about any statistic and chances are that Watson posted a career-best mark last season. It wasn't just that the 23-year-old forward averaged career highs in points, rebounds and assists; he also made 41% of his 3-pointers on a career-high volume and pulled off the rare feat of increasing his usage rate and true shooting percentage by large margins simultaneously.

In other words, Watson got many more opportunities last season, and he made the most of them.

The former No. 30 pick has always had potential, particularly on the defensive end, but he wasn't consistent or productive enough on offense to earn more playing time. In his playoff career, Watson has averaged only 10.4 minutes per game while receiving numerous DNPs.

That all changed last season. And although Watson didn't get the added opportunity to prove himself on the playoff stage because of a hamstring strain late in the year, he showed enough development in his breakout regular season -- as well as the potential for even more growth in the future -- to warrant a big raise in restricted free agency.

By itself, this is a perfectly reasonable new contract for a player with his youth and skill set. Before the offseason began, ESPN's Bobby Marks wrote that he'd offer Watson a four-year, $90 million deal, which is almost exactly what Cleveland ended up giving him.

Because Watson was a restricted free agent and Cleveland faced a financial strain, however, the Cavaliers couldn't sign Watson outright; instead, they needed to sacrifice Strus and a future unprotected first-round pick in the process.

On one hand, that cost is much more palatable than, say, what the Lakers paid in a similar trade for restricted free agent Walker Kessler earlier this summer.

But Strus was a valuable player for Cleveland, as both a proven 3-point shooter (37% in his career and with the Cavaliers) and solid defender. And that far-off future first-round pick could be valuable down the line, as well as hamper the Cavaliers' ability to make other trades in the years to come. (The Jazz already control their 2027, 2028 and 2029 firsts from the Donovan Mitchell blockbuster.)

Because of those extra considerations, this isn't a slam dunk A-plus deal for Cleveland; in a vacuum, Strus might even be a more valuable player than Watson right now. But it's easy to see -- and believe in -- the bet that the Cavaliers are making with this trade: that Watson provides much more upside than Strus, and that he's the wing who can finally bridge the positional gap between the Cavaliers' two All-Star guards and their two All-Star bigs.

In recent seasons, Cleveland has invested in and cycled through Strus, De'Andre Hunter, Caris LeVert, Dean Wade and Isaac Okoro, among others, in an effort to fill that void. None of those options truly succeeded. Now it's Watson's turn to try.

Grade for Nuggets: D

Given the extreme cost of the Nuggets roster that's already in place -- they're currently the only team in the second apron -- it's understandable why they didn't feel comfortable retaining Watson at such a price.

But letting him walk is a bitter pill to swallow for a Denver team that needed his youth and upside. The Nuggets just lost a key player, but they're a win-now team, with their top four players all entering their late primes: Nikola Jokic and Aaron Gordon will be 31 years old next season, Cameron Johnson will be 30 and Jamal Murray will be 29.

Moreover, the Nuggets have always been a thin team in the Jokic era, and they look even thinner following a quiet offseason. Of their top eight scorers last year, three have left the team this summer: Watson, Tim Hardaway Jr. and Jonas Valanciunas. And the only players they've brought in as replacements are Marvin Bagley III -- a questionable fit to follow Valanciunas as Jokic's backup -- and EuroLeague wing Alpha Diallo.

In the bigger picture, losing Watson means the Nuggets don't get to reap the long-term rewards of developing him from a raw reserve into a bona fide contributor. Amid a host of failed draft picks in the 25-40 range over the last half-decade -- Jalen Pickett, Julian Strawther, Hunter Tyson, Bones Hyland -- Watson was the one standout, and Denver clearly missed his two-way ability in its shocking playoff loss to the injury-ravaged Minnesota Timberwolves last spring.

But now the Cavaliers will benefit, because they were able to create enough financial wiggle room to dip below the second apron and add Watson, while the Nuggets were not.

The Nuggets' draft pick compensation is sufficiently enticing that this deal isn't an unmitigated disaster. Now the Nuggets, who didn't have any tradeable firsts before Wednesday, can theoretically use this unprotected Cavaliers pick to trade for a different player.

But will that player be better than Watson, who provided perimeter defense and athleticism otherwise lacking on the Nuggets' roster? And will that player fit any better into Denver's financial picture?

Depending on what they do with this pick, the Nuggets' front office could make this grade look silly in the coming months. But for now, it seems like they would have just been better off re-signing Watson.

Grade for Clippers: A-

Strus is signed for $16.6 million in 2026-27 before becoming a free agent next summer. That amount fits neatly onto the Clippers' books while keeping them below the tax line.

The Clippers are acquiring Strus on a short-term commitment, almost for free. Their only cost to add a proven 3-and-D veteran with ample playoff experience is a second-round pick they acquired from Philadelphia last month, in order to take on Johni Broome's salary.

That's a nice bit of business for the Clippers, even if it's still unclear where they fit into the Western Conference pecking order, or if they have any real ambitions for the 2026-27 season if the Kawhi Leonard trade goes through. If so, the Clippers' best course of action could be hoping they're able to re-trade Strus at the deadline for more draft compensation than the mere second-round pick with which they're parting in this deal.

Grade for Wizards: C+

The Wizards' angle in this deal is the least compelling, as they're getting a second-round pick and a minor upgrade at the guard position, via Mann, who first joined the Cavaliers last week in a trade for Dennis Schroder.

Aug. 14: Cavs trade Schroder to Hornets

Cleveland Cavaliers get: G Tre Mann

Charlotte Hornets get: G Dennis Schroder, cash considerations

Grade for Hornets: B-

Schroder is no stranger to changing teams: This deal represents the ninth time that the guard has been traded, and the Hornets will be his 12th team. Seven of those stops have come just since the 2023-24 season.

He has become an NBA vagabond for two main reasons. First, Schroder is a talented but inconsistent player, which means that he can improve a team's guard rotation (see: his stints with the Nets and Pistons in 2024-25) but isn't guaranteed to do so (see: his much less successful stint with the Warriors that season).

Second, the Sacramento Kings gave him a wildly over-market three-year, $44.4 million contract in a sign-and-trade last summer, which means he became a prime candidate to be traded from a team that needs to shed salary.

That's not an issue for the Hornets, however, who dumped a ton of money with their trades this summer. Schroder will make $14.8 million this season, or $6.8 million more than Mann's $8 million deal, and is signed for $15.5 million next season -- only $4.4 million of which is guaranteed.

The Hornets can stomach that cost. And in return, they bolstered their point guard depth, which was lacking after the blockbuster LaMelo Ball trade. Charlotte's only point guards before Friday's trade were Coby White (who's better suited as a combo guard than pure point), rookie Christian Anderson and Mann. But Mann was a mere bit player last season, averaging 5.5 points in 12.6 minutes per game.

Because Schroder will turn 33 next month and has already run hot and cold for years, it's unclear how much of an upgrade he'll be in Charlotte, which is why the Hornets don't grade out even better for this deal. They also didn't pick up any draft picks in the process. In contrast, they received an A-minus for taking on Dorian Finney-Smith's contract -- along with three second-round picks -- from the Rockets.

But compared with Mann and an unproven rookie, Schroder should provide better depth for the Hornets next season. And if not, well, Schroder has already been traded in February in four of the past five years, so Charlotte could always try to spin him off to yet another team at the deadline.

Grade for Cavaliers: B

For Cleveland, trading Schroder -- whom the team initially acquired in a dual salary dump involving De'Andre Hunter -- is all about money. Saving the $6.8 million difference between Schroder's and Mann's salaries places Cleveland roughly $32 million below the first apron and $44 million below the second apron, according to ESPN's Bobby Marks.

That seems like a lot of room already -- but the expected new contract for James Harden should eat into much of that space. So an extra chunk of change could make a big difference if Cleveland intends to pursue other meaningful additions, such as restricted free agent Peyton Watson or unrestricted free agent Jonathan Kuminga.

And after a rough playoff showing, during which Schroder averaged 5.5 points in 15.9 minutes per game on 50% true shooting, the Cavaliers shouldn't miss his on-court contributions too dearly. With Harden presumably rejoining the team and Donovan Mitchell firmly rooted in Cleveland, the Cavaliers have less need for the ballhandling and creation Schroder provides.

They should be able to distribute his playing time to younger players whose superior shooting strokes are a better fit around Harden and Mitchell regardless.

July 19: Lu Dort dealt to Hawks in three-team deal
Atlanta Hawks get: G Luguentz Dort, G Ryan Nembhard

Dallas Mavericks get: F Zaccharie Risacher

Oklahoma City Thunder get: Three future second-round picks

Grade for Oklahoma City: B-

What this means for Thunder: Oklahoma City's offseason of financial maneuvers might finally be complete now that the team has traded Dort, Aaron Wiggins and Isaiah Joe to limbo beneath the second apron threshold. Those moves will save the Thunder more than $300 million next season, between those players' salaries and their tax savings, as well as avoid the second apron's harsh roster restrictions for another year.

But this trade is materially different from the Thunder's other salary dumps this summer. Wiggins and Joe are solid role players who were nonetheless luxuries on Oklahoma City's stacked roster; they ranked 10th and 11th on the team, respectively, in playoff minutes over the past two seasons.

Dort, conversely, was a vital member of the team that won the 2024-25 championship and finished with the league's best record in 2025-26. He ranked third on the Thunder in playoff minutes over the past two seasons, and he started every playoff game.

He may still have been the most expendable member of Oklahoma City's core. Cason Wallace is younger than Dort, with more offensive zest in his game. And while he isn't an elite defender in exactly the same way -- Wallace causes more turnovers, while Dort is more physically imposing -- he can step right into Dort's spot defending the best guard on opposing teams.

Moreover, between Wallace, Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, Jalen Williams, Alex Caruso, Ajay Mitchell and Jared McCain, the Thunder are still loaded on the perimeter, even after their three trades this summer. That's different from the center position, where Isaiah Hartenstein still offers irreplaceable two-way production; so if the Thunder had to choose between keeping Dort and Hartenstein, as seemed likely when both players entered this summer on team options, then Hartenstein was always the more obvious choice.

That's doubly true when considering Oklahoma City's chief competition atop the Western Conference. Hartenstein was the Thunder's best option against the Spurs' Victor Wembanyama in the conference finals, while Dort didn't really have a place against San Antonio's guards.

If anything, Dort was a weak link against a Spurs team that left him open on the perimeter. He fell to seventh on the Thunder in minutes in the conference finals, and the Thunder had a minus-63 point differential with him on the court, which was by far the worst for any player in the series.

Trading Dort now, with just a year left on his contract, gives the Thunder more draft assets and clears more cap space to extend Wallace and Mitchell, without necessarily making the team worse against San Antonio.

Yet that optimistic view of the tradeoffs doesn't mean this is a risk-free deal. Dort might not have the same upside as other players on the Thunder roster, but he's almost always available -- at least 69 games in each of the past five seasons, with zero missed playoff games -- and offers a high, firm floor.

Because the young Thunder guards -- McCain and Mitchell, plus Nikola Topic and Bennett Stirtz, to the extent that they'll play this season -- lean more toward the offensive side, Oklahoma City is now just one Wallace injury away from defensive cracks appearing on the perimeter for the first time in the team's current run of contention.

Losing Dort, as well as depth options Wiggins and Joe, will make the Thunder worse in the 2026-27 regular season; such is life in a second apron world. They're betting that their playoff quality will remain high enough to justify the cost savings and asset reallocation that this trade provides. That bet may well pay off, but it's also the riskiest one the Thunder have made in a couple of years.

Grade for Atlanta: A-

What this means for Hawks: Atlanta continues a strong offseason with another shrewd trade. It wouldn't seem that way based on the draft pedigrees of the three players involved in this trade, as Risacher was a No. 1 pick and both Dort and Nembhard were undrafted.

Ignore the draft record, though, and Dort is clearly a more valuable player, both in the present and future, than Risacher. The 27-year-old wing is still in his prime age range and only a year removed from being named to the All-Defensive first team, where he joined Dyson Daniels, now his new teammate in Atlanta.

Whether Dort and Daniels can function together offensively remains to be seen, but between Dort, Daniels and Nickeil Alexander-Walker, Atlanta now boasts one of the best defensive trios in the NBA. The Hawks finished 10th in defensive rating last season and could easily push into the top five in 2026-27.

Dort also gives the Hawks another useful rotation player, period, which is a necessity for Atlanta to improve next season. As I wrote when analyzing Atlanta's trade for another Thunder player, Wiggins, the Hawks ended last postseason with what was effectively a six-man rotation, and one of those six players (Jonathan Kuminga) won't be back. Dort and Wiggins on the wings, plus Nembhard and No. 8 pick Kingston Flemings in the backcourt, should help address that weakness.

As for the price to acquire Dort, it's possible that giving up on Risacher this early will prove foolish in the long run. He's a 6-foot-8 wing who's still just 21 years old, which makes him among the most valuable player archetypes in the NBA.

But Risacher is fairly expensive ($13.8 million in 2026-27, with a $17.4 million team option for 2027-28), and he hasn't looked the part of a future star, or even a future starter for a contender, in his NBA career to date. His statistics were essentially the same or slightly worse across the board in his second season compared to his first, showing little development, and he'd lost the trust of Atlanta coach Quin Snyder.

Risacher played just 23 total minutes in the playoffs, and the majority of those came in the second half of the 51-point blowout loss that ended Atlanta's season.

Out of 41 No. 1 picks in the lottery era, Risacher ranked 39th in box plus/minus through each player's first two seasons, per Stathead, ahead of only infamous draft busts Anthony Bennett and Michael Olowokandi.

Typically, a future contributor has demonstrated more evidence of his ability on the court by this point in his career. Andrew Wiggins -- whose BPM was still much better than Risacher's -- is the only success story among the players at the bottom of this list.

If this were a retrospective draft grade, the Hawks would receive failing marks for selecting Risacher at No. 1 instead of Alex Sarr (who went second) or Stephon Castle (who went fourth). But Atlanta viewed that mistake as a sunk cost and turned Risacher into a better player in this trade.

Grade for Dallas: B+

What this means for Mavericks: This is a simple talent play for Dallas, which traded a small undrafted guard for a 6-foot-8 2024 No. 1 pick, who's two years younger to boot. Nembhard was a fine backup point guard who helped stabilize a turnover-prone backcourt last season, and Risacher doesn't help alleviate Dallas' glut of forwards -- but this exchange makes perfect sense for the upside alone.

Whether or not Risacher looks better in his new environment, this is a strong process move for a team in need of young talent around Cooper Flagg, with little future draft capital on the way. With Risacher and Flagg, the Mavericks now have the No. 1 picks from both the 2024 and 2025 drafts.

Risacher will slot into the Anthony Davis trade exception, and Dallas now has a season to watch him develop before deciding whether to extend him next summer or let him reach restricted free agency in 2028.

July 7: Pistons trade LeVert to Bucks for Prince, Harris
Milwaukee Bucks get: Caris LeVert, two second-round picks

Detroit Pistons get: Gary Harris, Taurean Prince

Grade for Detroit: B-

What this means for the Pistons: Within the last week, the Memphis Grizzlies traded Santi Aldama and the Houston Rockets traded Dorian Finney-Smith, and now the Pistons join the party with LeVert. The common thread between those three transactions is that all three teams signed those players last summer, only to want a mulligan a year later.

LeVert's two-year, $28.9 million deal with Detroit was a bust from the start. He averaged a career-low 7.4 points last season, as his true shooting declined from 58% in 2024-25 to just 52% last season.

Things didn't get much better in the playoffs, even as coach J.B. Bickerstaff turned to LeVert -- who ranked seventh on the team in playoff minutes -- in his search for more offense. The veteran wing reached double-digit points only twice in the postseason and averaged 5.9 points in the playoffs; he didn't play in Detroit's Game 7 win over the Orlando Magic.

Harris and Prince won't be much more help on the court for Detroit if they even stay on the team into the season. Harris averaged 2.7 points last season. Prince was more productive but appeared in only 26 games.

But this trade is chiefly motivated by finances. To shed LeVert's contract and save $7.2 million -- the balance of LeVert's salary minus Harris' and Prince's $3.8 million apiece -- Detroit had to give up two second-round picks. That seems like a fair price, given that Houston sent Charlotte three second-rounders to save $13.3 million in the Finney-Smith trade.

How the Pistons end up using that extra wiggle room remains to be seen, but despite trading for Isaiah Joe, trading Isaiah Stewart, re-signing Kevin Huerter and swapping John Collins for Tobias Harris, their to-do list is still crowded. Jalen Duren lingers in restricted free agency, and the Pistons haven't added a true second scorer who can make Cade Cunningham's life easier.

Grade for Milwaukee: B+

What this means for the Bucks: Before this trade, the rebuilding Bucks didn't have second-round picks in 2027, 2028, 2029, 2030, 2031 or 2032, so suffice it to say that a couple of draft assets from Detroit are more valuable in Milwaukee than just about anywhere else in the NBA.

That's the thrust of the trade for Milwaukee, which doesn't have much use for declining veterans in their 30s -- a description that characterizes all three players in this trade.

In another city, in another time, LeVert might have received a chance to bounce back as a scorer for a rebuilding team. But that's not the most likely outcome here: If LeVert stays in Milwaukee, he'll join a crowded perimeter rotation that already included Ryan Rollins, Tyler Herro, Jaime Jaquez Jr., Kevin Porter Jr., Kasparas Jakucionis and lottery pick Brayden Burries. Odds are that at least one of those players, perhaps more, won't still be on Milwaukee's roster by opening night.

July 3: Lakers trade Ayton to Wizards for Hardy, picks

Washington Wizards get: Deandre Ayton

Los Angeles Lakers get: Jaden Hardy, two second-round picks (in 2031 and 2032)

Grade for Washington: C

What this means for the Wizards: After replacing Anthony Davis as the Lakers' center, Ayton is now joining him in Washington. Add in AJ Dybantsa and Alex Sarr, and that's three No. 1 picks and a No. 2 pick all crammed into Washington's frontcourt, as well as former No. 2 pick D'Angelo Russell still on the roster, as well.

Ayton hasn't looked like a No. 1 pick for a while, of course, but the Wizards aren't expecting him to. Instead, they're hoping he'll "provide insurance for Washington's front line while Sarr recovers" from offseason foot surgery, per ESPN's Dave McMenamin.

He can do so credibly enough, and he'd become especially important to the front line if the Wizards end up trading Davis at some point before next summer, when he could become a free agent if he opts out of his $62.8 million player option. Ayton averaged 12.5 points and 8.0 rebounds per game last season.

But there are two confusing aspects to the Wizards' side of this trade. The first is what it says about their view of Sarr, who played 100% of his minutes as the Wizards' center last season, per Cleaning the Glass' positional breakdown. Sarr's average shot distance moved from 14.4 feet away in his rookie season to 10.5 feet away last season, and his numbers skyrocketed as a result.

With Davis and Ayton on the roster, though, the Wizards seem set on using Sarr as a power forward and crowding his space inside with other non-shooting big men.

The second confusing factor concerns the opportunity cost of trading draft capital and Hardy -- who averaged 22.2 points per 36 minutes and made 42% of his 3-pointers after a midseason trade to the Wizards last season -- when similar centers to Ayton are freely available.

One such player is already on the Wizards' roster: 23-year-old Tristan Vukcevic is a younger, lower-cost option to Ayton ($3 million this season, with a team option for the same amount next season), who quietly filled up the stat sheet last season. The 7-foot Italian averaged 23.7 points per 36 minutes and made 35% of his 3s on high volume.

Ayton is a former No. 1 pick, but there's a reason he's moving to his fourth team in five years. In the first four seasons of his career, Ayton had a positive on/off rating, meaning his team was better with him on the floor. But in three of the past four seasons, Ayton has had a severely negative on/off rating.

Last season, the Lakers were minus-0.4 points per 100 possessions when Ayton played, per Cleaning the Glass, versus plus-5.3 when he didn't.

Grade for Los Angeles: B

What this means for the Lakers: Ayton seemed like an obvious trade candidate as soon as he opted in to his $8.1 million player option for 2026-27, and especially so after the Lakers added Walker Kessler in a pricey sign-and-trade.

Dealing Ayton saves the Lakers $2.1 million -- the difference between his and Hardy's salaries -- which they'll use to help fit their flurry of free agent signings into their cap space. And with Kessler receiving the majority of minutes at center, the backup role should be easily filled on the free agent market, with "centers such as Andre Drummond, Jonas Valanciunas and Kevon Looney among those being considered," according to ESPN's Shams Charania.

The Lakers' return from Washington, meanwhile, is minor but shouldn't be overlooked. Hardy could help the Lakers, based on his surge down the stretch last season, or he could be dealt to help fill another roster hole. And the addition of two second-round picks gives the Lakers crucial draft capital they can use in other deals, because until Friday, all they had left was one first-round pick (in 2032) they could swap and one second-round pick (in 2033) they could trade.

Ayton puts up better box score stats than the caliber of backup center who will replace him, and his loss means the Lakers are even more dependent on Kessler staying healthy, after committing so many resources to a center who appeared in just five games last season. But the added financial and draft flexibility from this exchange makes it well worth it for the Lakers.

July 3: Hornets acquiring Finney-Smith, picks from Rockets

Charlotte Hornets get: Dorian Finney-Smith, three second-round picks (via Memphis in 2027, Houston in 2028 and Houston in 2033)

Houston Rockets get: $13 million trade exception

Grade for Houston: C

What this means for the Rockets: Continuing the trend of teams taking mulligans on deals they handed out last summer, Houston is trading Finney-Smith in a salary dump, which will allow the Rockets to move out of both the first apron and luxury tax.

Finney-Smith seemed like a shrewd pickup last summer, but he missed the start of the 2025-26 season after ankle surgery and never found his footing in Houston. He averaged only 3.3 points per game on 27% 3-point shooting, just a year after scoring 8.7 PPG and making 41% of his 3s.

The financial impetus for the Rockets' side of this trade makes sense, after they negotiated smart deals with free agents Marcus Smart and Tari Eason. But three second-round picks is a fairly heavy price to pay to get off Finney-Smith's contract, which is only guaranteed for one more year at $13.3 million.

Houston is now out of second-round picks from 2028 through 2033, save the back end of one unfavorable swap in 2031. That hole could hamper the team's ability to add low-cost talent for the near future, but even more importantly, second-round picks are a key asset to grease the wheel for trades.

The Rockets have extra first-round picks in 2027 and 2029, and they own all of their own firsts for the next seven years. But making minor trades could be a bit more challenging going forward.

Grade for Charlotte: A-

What this means for the Hornets: Finney-Smith failed to launch in Houston, but he was a standout role player as recently as the 2024-25 season, due to his 3-and-D skill set and excellent on/off rating. Now 33 years old, Finney-Smith might just be done as an NBA rotation player, but he's also a reasonable bounce-back candidate from an injury-marred season, and could very well be a contributor in Charlotte.

If he does bounce back, the Hornets can keep him around for another $13.3 million in 2027-28. If not, they can let him go with no penalty because his contract is only guaranteed for this upcoming season -- Charlotte can easily afford him in 2025-26 after opening up oodles of cap space with its trades of LaMelo Ball and Miles Bridges.

That's a win-win proposition for the Hornets, who picked up three second-round picks for facilitating Houston's cap maneuver. Charlotte now has 20 second-round picks over the next seven years.

At some point, there are diminishing returns on such a large haul; is there anything the Hornets can accomplish with 20 second-rounders that they couldn't with 17?

But between their collection of draft assets and their financial flexibility, the Hornets are in prime position to make just about any transaction they want in the years to come. In the modern NBA, that optionality is a prize in and of itself.

July 1: Celtics trade Jaylen Brown to Sixers for Paul George, picks

Boston Celtics get: F Paul George, 2028 first-round pick (could convert to a pick swap), 2031 first-round pick (unprotected), 2028 and 2030 second-round picks

Philadelphia 76ers get: G Jaylen Brown

Grade for Boston: D+

What this means for Celtics: Here's a hot take, right off the bat: The Celtics might very well win 50-plus games again next season. After all, they went 56-26 last season despite playing only 16 games with Jayson Tatum, who was recovering from a torn Achilles.

If Tatum is fully healthy next season, he could mimic Brown's 2025-26 production. And the Celtics have otherwise improved this summer, as they added Mitchell Robinson and have thus far retained the rest of the core that powered their surprisingly strong season.

Yet that's a glib way to start this analysis, because swapping Brown for George makes the Celtics worse. It clearly makes them worse. Crucially, it lowers their playoff ceiling, even if the likes of Hugo Gonzalez, Baylor Scheierman and Jordan Walsh might mash together enough solid minutes to try to replace the departed All-Star throughout the regular season.

It's utterly strange that the Celtics would willingly take such a giant step back. This is the most successful franchise of the decade: In the 2020s, they rank first in regular-season wins and playoff wins, and they're the only team to both win a championship and make another Finals.

Grade for Philadelphia: A-

What this means for 76ers: Brown could be a very good fit in Philadelphia. The 76ers have two excellent guards, Tyrese Maxey and VJ Edgecombe, and one excellent-when-healthy center, Joel Embiid. But they've never had adequate forwards to connect those positional strengths, and George on a maximum contract was evidently not the answer.

Dean Wade seemed like a worthwhile solution when the 76ers agreed to a four-year deal with him Tuesday. But Brown is on a completely different level from anyone the 76ers have tried there before. He can handle more of the scoring load when the oft-injured Embiid misses time, operate as a secondary playmaker next to Maxey and provide strong perimeter defense, particularly if he's not expending so much of his energy on the offensive end.

Brown could also be a very awkward fit in Philadelphia. He hasn't played with an elite ball-dominant point guard in years, since Kyrie Irving's fairly disastrous tenure in Boston, and he has never played with a post presence like Embiid.

July 1: Lakers give up picks to get Kessler from Jazz
Utah Jazz get: Two unprotected first-round picks (2031, 2033), two first-round swaps (2028, 2030)

Los Angeles Lakers get: C Walker Kessler

Grade for Utah: A+

What this means for the Jazz: As a player, Utah Jazz CEO Danny Ainge beat the Lakers in the 1984 Finals, and he eliminated the Lakers from the playoffs in both 1992 and 1993. As an executive, he beat the Lakers for another title, in 2008.

So it's saying something that this deal is one of the biggest wins Ainge has ever had over the purple and gold.

The Jazz need a center, so losing Kessler hurts. Jusuf Nurkic -- re-signed to a two-year deal -- shouldn't start for a contender at this point in his career, and Jaren Jackson Jr. has played his best basketball as a power forward next to another true big man. (With Kessler departing before he and Jackson could ever play a game together, the Jazz will never get to see how many blocks that duo could have collected.)

But there was simply no way Utah could turn down receiving two unprotected first-round picks and two pick swaps, and not having to increase their contract offer to Kessler beyond where they felt comfortable. Given his uncertain potential, Kessler might not be worth this contract anyway, and Utah was paid handsomely to let him go at that price.

The Jazz received more draft capital for Kessler than the Clippers did for Kawhi Leonard, and more than the Hornets did for LaMelo Ball. Heck, they received more draft capital than the Cavaliers received in the most famous sign-and-trade this century, when they landed two first-round picks and one swap in LeBron James' "Decision." Kessler is a valuable young center, but he's not a star.

They now have ample optionality as they decide how to replace Kessler. They could try playing Jackson at center and Lauri Markkanen at power forward, then add another center if necessary. Or they could aim for a stopgap solution next to Nurkic and use their immense pick stash to target and trade for a better long-term fit.

Those solutions likely won't be as clean or immediate as re-signing Kessler would have been, so it's fair to downgrade Utah's chances at vaulting up the standings and into the playoff field as a result of this trade. But in the bigger picture, the Jazz received tremendous value. They received the first A-plus grade for any deal this offseason.

Grade for Los Angeles: C-

What this means for the Lakers: As if it weren't clear already, the back-to-back news breaks of LeBron James leaving the Lakers on Tuesday and the team acquiring Kessler on Wednesday definitely prove that this is Luka Doncic's team now.

Chief among the player archetypes proven to work next to Doncic is a rim-running, rim-protecting center, and the 24-year-old Kessler is an ideal player in that role.

If Victor Wembanyama didn't exist, Kessler might be considered the best rim protector in the world. The 7-foot-2 center ranks second among active players (behind Wembanyama) with a career 8.3% block rate. And he ranks third over the course of his career (behind Chet Holmgren and Wembanyama, among players with at least 500 shots defended) by allowing opponents to shoot just 54.6% in the restricted area when he's the closest defender, per GeniusIQ.

On the other end of the floor, Kessler is a more limited scorer, but more than a third of his career shot attempts are dunks, per Basketball Reference -- which explains why he's a 68% career shooter. He'll surely add plenty more slams as he partners with Doncic in the seasons to come.

Kessler hasn't typically had much success as a screen-setter. In his last full season (2024-25), his team scored just 0.85 points per play directly out of his screens, per GeniusIQ. That ranked dead last -- 46th out of 46 players with at least 1,000 screens set -- in efficiency.

But that ranking comes with a major caveat, of course: The ball handlers who were playing off those Kessler picks were the likes of pre-breakout Keyonte George, Collin Sexton and Isaiah Collier. It's safe to say Doncic and Austin Reaves will be significantly more effective partners.

Kessler also led the league in offensive rebounds in 2024-25, with 4.6 per game, so he'll provide a new element to an offense that ranked 24th in offensive rebounding rate last season.

He's even stretching his range out to the 3-point line. He went 6-for-8 from distance in five games last season, after making just six total 3s (out of 34 attempts) in 2024-25. I watched film of all 64 of Kessler's career 3-point attempts, and he has improved his form over time. Earlier in his career, his left elbow placement was erratic, with a tendency to wobble, but it looked more consistent in last season's small sample.

Despite all of those strengths, and despite Kessler's theoretically perfect fit next to Doncic, however, the Lakers are paying an outrageous price to acquire him.

It's not as if Kessler is a proven All-Star. In that respect, this deal is more like the Mikal Bridges and Desmond Bane trades -- which exchanged buckets of picks for non-All-Stars -- than, say, the Lakers' trade for Anthony Davis in 2019.

There are still so many unknowns about Kessler's true quality as a two-way center. For instance, his shooting touch is largely theoretical; you'd have to place a lot of stock in last season's tiny sample to trust he's meaningfully improved from his 20% 3-point accuracy and 54% free throw accuracy from his first three seasons.

Maybe that won't matter as much on the Lakers, where all he'll need to do on offense is set screens and score the easy baskets that Doncic sets up for him. But then he won't be worth the $32.5 million per year, with a player option and trade kicker, that the Lakers are giving him; they could find a dunker who can protect the rim for a much cheaper price.

Kessler was generally healthy before last season, when a torn labrum ended his campaign after just five games, but he also hasn't played a meaningful game in his NBA career. He went to Utah as a draft pick in the Rudy Gobert trade, right as the Jazz were starting an extended swoon.

How Kessler interacts with the Lakers' future flexibility is interesting. On the one hand, there was some urgency for GM Rob Pelinka to find his center of the future now, as this was the Lakers' last offseason to use their cap space in a meaningful way before they'll have Doncic and Reaves on the books for more than half of the cap.

But on the other hand, Pelinka sacrificed nearly all his future draft flexibility by committing not only to give Kessler a contract at the very top of his market, but also to give the Jazz control of four future picks in the process. The Lakers already owed a top-four-protected pick to Memphis in 2027 and an unprotected first-rounder to Dallas in 2029, and they don't have any second-round picks until 2033.

They are now effectively out of picks they can use to make further roster upgrades for several years. This trade had better work out and elevate the Lakers to true championship contention, because they're now all-in on the Doncic-Reaves-Kessler core.

July 1: Mavs add Santi Aldama in trade from Grizzlies
Dallas Mavericks get: F Santi Aldama

Memphis Grizzlies get: G AJ Johnson, 2030 first-round pick (via Warriors, top-20 protected), two second-round picks

Memphis: B+

What this means for Grizzlies: This trade represents a case of having second thoughts for the Grizzlies, who signed Aldama to a three-year, $52.5 million deal last summer.

Aldama is a perfectly acceptable NBA player, as a 7-footer with legitimate shooting range and an eagerness to score. He averaged a career-high 14 points in 41 games last season, before his season ended early because of a right knee injury.

But even though the Grizzlies traded Jaren Jackson Jr. last season, they've also added several power forwards since, drafting Cameron Boozer with the third pick and acquiring Jerami Grant in the Ja Morant trade. Memphis also traded for Isaiah Stewart from Detroit, leaving the Grizzlies with three frontcourt players who deserve more playing time than the 25-year-old Spaniard.

Trading Aldama helps clear up that logjam, frees a roster spot (Johnson is a candidate to be cut) and saves Memphis some money. Aldama is owed $17 million next season and another $17 million (on a team option) in 2027-28.

Dallas: C+

What this means for Mavericks: In a strange bit of circumstance, Aldama is essentially serving as the Mavericks' delayed return from their trade of Anthony Davis, half a year after they dealt him to Washington. In that exchange, Dallas received, among other assets, this protected Warriors pick, Johnson and a trade exception that they're now using to acquire Aldama.

Aldama is obviously an inferior player to Davis, a 10-time All-Star (and to Luka Doncic, whom Dallas initially traded for Davis). But that's not the fairest way to view this trade. Aldama is a clear talent upgrade to Johnson, and he'll make the Mavericks better next season with the addition of his size and shooting.

But just as Aldama's departure cleared a positional logjam in Memphis, his arrival is adding to one in Dallas. The Mavericks have Aldama, P.J. Washington, Cooper Flagg and No. 9 pick Morez Johnson Jr. on their roster -- and all four players might be best suited for power forward.

Dallas' most important priority should be optimizing Flagg's development, but barring further moves, he's unlikely to spend much time at the 4 next season. That might not be a huge deal in the grand scheme of the Mavericks' future, but it's also not the best use of a rotation spot, either.

June 30: Raptors reunite with Leonard in trade with Clippers
Toronto Raptors get: F Kawhi Leonard

LA Clippers get: F Brandon Ingram, G Gradey Dick, two unprotected first-round picks, one pick swap, two second-round picks

Grade for Toronto: A-

What this means for the Raptors: When he's available, Leonard remains one of the NBA's best players. Remarkably, the 34-year-old seven-time All-Star averaged a career-high 27.9 points per game on a career-high usage rate last season. LeBron James is the only player in NBA history with a better box plus/minus at that age or older.

Leonard's offensive gifts have scarcely departed him despite his age and injury history. Since returning from an ACL tear that cost him the entire 2021-22 campaign, he has made 40.5% of his 3-pointers. For context, Stephen Curry's at 40.6% over the same span. And out of 60 players over the past four seasons with at least a 25% usage rate, Leonard ranks 10th in true shooting percentage, despite a difficult shot diet.

He is also the rare No. 1 option on offense who is equally adept on the other end, even if the two-time Defensive Player of the Year is no longer at his peak on every possession. Leonard still averaged 1.9 steals per game last season, a top-five mark in the league. The other players in the top five were all 25 years old or younger.

Grade for LA: B

What this means for the Clippers: The Clippers have quietly been stuck in the middle even more than Toronto. They haven't won a playoff series since 2021, and in all five seasons since, they've finished with a winning record but lost in the play-in round twice and the first round of the proper playoffs thrice.

In response to all that mediocrity, the front office has actively disassembled the team's core over the past couple of years. The Clippers' top 16 scorers from the 2022-23 team that won 51 games have all cycled off the roster. That exodus includes some departures via free agency (most notably Paul George), but mostly a succession of trades: of Russell Westbrook, then Norman Powell, then James Harden, then Ivica Zubac and now Leonard.

All of those transactions have wrought dramatic changes to the roster. The Clippers were the NBA's oldest team in each of the past three seasons, per Basketball Reference. But they should get much younger in a hurry, as they pursue a complete rebuild around the backcourt duo of Darius Garland and No. 5 pick Keaton Wagler. With Leonard gone, 38-year-old Brook Lopez and 32-year-old Kris Dunn are the only remaining Clippers in their 30s.
