June 29: Grizzlies trade Morant to Blazers
Memphis Grizzlies get: F Jerami Grant, F Kris Murray

Portland Trail Blazers get: G Ja Morant

Grade for Portland: B-

What this means for the Trail Blazers: Ja Morant is a two-time All-Star and a Most Improved Player winner, who once ranked among the most electric young talents in the league. But there are several reasons that the 26-year-old guard was available for such a reasonable trade price -- so low that Portland didn't have to include picks in this deal.

Morant has been suspended multiple times in the past few seasons, most notably for displaying a firearm on an Instagram Live stream. He also underwent right shoulder surgery for a labral tear in January 2024.

And even when he has been available to play, Morant has faced major hurdles over the past few seasons that have kept him from reemerging as an elite offensive engine.

The first is Morant's lack of development as a shooter; his 3-point percentage peaked in 2021-22 at just 34%. His career 31% 3-point mark ranks 189th out of 194 active players with at least 1,000 attempts, per Stathead.

Players below him include Russell Westbrook and Giannis Antetokounmpo, who both have starred despite their unreliable 3-point strokes. But Westbrook and Antetokounmpo combined spectacular athleticism with dominant scoring near the basket, and Morant has also declined in those areas since his early peak.

Morant ranked among the league leaders in made baskets in the restricted area in 2021-22. That was an impressive feat because, according to GeniusIQ, every other player near the top of that leaderboard was a center or a big physical forward, such as Antetokounmpo and LeBron James. But Morant has made progressively fewer shots near the rim in every season since.

It is a massive question whether Morant can help the Trail Blazers, and if his potential can manifest again in stellar offensive production and All-Star-level play.

Though Portland hadn't been rumored to have interest in Morant before Monday, this destination makes sense for him. For large stretches of this past season, injuries left Portland without a point guard, and that had some strange effects. Forward Deni Avdija led the team in time of possession, for instance, and the Trail Blazers had the highest turnover rate in the league.

But now, the Trail Blazers will go for a bulk approach at point guard, with Morant, Damian Lillard, Scoot Henderson and Jrue Holiday all capable of playing the position, though trading Grant means they have almost no frontcourt depth. Other than the defensively sound, positionally malleable Holiday, those players don't make much sense playing together; there's not enough shooting or defense in that group.

But between their injury risks and potential further trades -- the Trail Blazers might be more comfortable trading Holiday for a star such as Jaylen Brown -- this logjam might not be as much of an issue as it appears. And if the Trail Blazers are eager to play Henderson off the ball, as he did while recording 59 shots and just six assists in the postseason, then Morant and Lillard could split point guard duties without too much difficulty.

The greater risk for the Trail Blazers might be how their new acquisition fits over the long term, even though they didn't have to surrender picks. At the 2026 trade deadline, the Wizards also didn't have to trade picks to acquire Trae Young -- but they turned a low-cost move into a high-cost maneuver by extending him for four years and $212 million.

That outcome seems unlikely in Portland, though; don't expect a Morant extension soon. Instead, wait to see if this move allows Morant to return to even a semblance of the stardom he once enjoyed in Memphis. It's not likely, but it's not impossible.

Grade for Memphis: B

What this means for the Grizzlies: Morant's standing had fallen so far in the league, his weaknesses growing more and more glaring, that it's not a surprise that the Grizzlies receive more in trade return. Instead, they dealt one undesirable contract for another, exchanging Grant's two-year deal for Morant's.

Grant had fallen behind Avdija and Toumani Camara in Portland's rotation. Grant can still score (18.6 points per game this past season) and make 3-pointers (39% last season), but his star has lost its luster as he has slipped defensively and suffered a litany of injuries. Grant hasn't played more than 63 games in a season since 2020.

Meanwhile, Murray, the No. 23 pick in the 2023 draft, has averaged 5.3 points in 188 games. It's difficult for a perimeter player to succeed as a 26% career 3-point shooter.

Looking ahead, Grant will make $34.2 million in 2026-27 and has a $36.4 million player option in 2027-28, while Morant is owed $42.2 million in 2026-27 and $44.9 million in 2027-28 on the maximum rookie extension he signed in 2022, right after the best season of his career.

That amounts to about $8 million in savings in each of the next two seasons for Memphis, assuming Grant picks up his option.

That's not a lot -- but frankly, it could be a win for Memphis not to have to give up draft capital to incentivize another team to take on Morant's deal and drama.

Morant's departure completes the teardown of what briefly appeared to be the best young core in the NBA, as the Grizzlies have traded Desmond Bane, Jaren Jackson Jr. and Morant over the past 12 months. That trio won 56 games in 2021-22 and 51 more in 2022-23, landing the No. 2 seed in the West both years, but won just one playoff series together.

The end of that era came with a whimper. Now, the Grizzlies can pivot to a future led by Cameron Boozer, Cedric Coward and Zach Edey, a new young trio to replace the former one.

June 28: Hornets deal Bridges, picks to Suns
Charlotte Hornets get: G Grayson Allen, F Royce O'Neale, 2033 unprotected first-round pick

Phoenix Suns get: F Miles Bridges, 2027 second-round pick (least favorable of Boston and Orlando), 2029 first-round pick (least favorable of Charlotte, Utah, Cleveland and Minnesota)

Grade for Charlotte: B+

What this means for the Hornets: Just a few days ago, the Hornets made the surprising decision to remove one member of last season's best five-man lineup, by trading LaMelo Ball to Minnesota. Apparently, they weren't done breaking up that band.

It makes sense to think of this trade as a natural follow-up to the Ball blockbuster, which brought Naz Reid to Charlotte along with draft capital, including an unprotected first-round pick in 2033.

Adding Reid gave the Hornets four big men with diverse skill sets, all of whom are either solid NBA players already (Reid and Moussa Diabate) or recent draft picks who need playing time (Ryan Kalkbrenner and Hannes Steinbach). All four are also younger than Bridges.

So with Reid's ability to play power forward, where he'll now start for the first extended stretch of his career, Bridges had lost his spot. And the Hornets cashed in by acquiring another unprotected first-round pick in 2033. That's reason enough to make this deal, especially because it came at the cost of a player with just one remaining season on his contract, whom the Hornets might not have wanted to extend.

It will also be interesting to see how much Allen and O'Neale are able to give the Hornets on the court, after Phoenix included them in this deal primarily for cost-cutting purposes.

Allen is coming off a season to forget: He made just 35% of his 3-pointers -- after finishing well above 40% in his previous two campaigns -- and missed part of Phoenix's playoff loss because of a hamstring strain. Given that he'll turn 31 years old before the start of next season, he's clearly on the downslope of his career. But if his shot bounces back to its typical level, he can still help a team that led the league in made 3-pointers last season, but has since lost Ball.

O'Neale, meanwhile, has been an available and serviceable role player for years. He hasn't missed more than seven games in any season since he was a rookie (2017-18), and he has made 41% of his 3-pointers on high volume over the past two seasons (39% in his career). He'll fit nicely on Charlotte's bench.

The Hornets probably wish they weren't paying that duo in the neighborhood of $30 million per year to come off the bench. But that's a price worth paying to add to their growing pick stash.

Grade for Phoenix: D+

What this means for the Suns: Here is a list of NBA players who have been traded for at least one unprotected first-round pick so far this summer: Giannis Antetokounmpo, LaMelo Ball and Bridges. Antetokounmpo is a two-time MVP. Ball is a former All-Star and Rookie of the Year who's still just 24 years old. Bridges, meanwhile, is a 28-year-old forward who has never come close to making an All-Star squad.

That makes for a strange use of an unprotected pick, for a team that already has very little draft capital: The Suns had previously traded their first-round picks in 2027, 2029 and 2031, and they'd traded swap rights in 2028 and 2030.

Until this week, they were unable to trade any further picks outright, due to the Stepien rule that prevents teams from trading first-round picks in consecutive drafts. But now that 2033 picks can go for sale -- teams can trade picks from up to seven drafts in advance -- the Suns got rid of theirs with the utmost haste.

In return, they acquired Bridges, who in 2022 was sentenced to three years of probation after pleading no contest to a felony domestic violence charge of injuring a child's parent. He didn't play in the 2022-23 season and was further suspended for the first 10 games of 2023-24.

Since his return, Bridges has put up box score stats, but his raw scoring totals (17.1 points per game last season) overstate his impact. Advanced stats rate him as a roughly average player.

Bridges will add size to a small Suns perimeter rotation, but there are a few problems with his fit on a winning team. The first is his defense; the Hornets have typically had a worse defensive rating with him on the floor versus when he's off.

Bridges is not a very active defender. He averaged just 1.2 steals plus blocks per 36 minutes last season, which ranked 248th out of 279 players with at least 1,000 minutes. Many of the players below him are offensive specialists, either on-ball stars (Jalen Brunson, Devin Booker, Zach LaVine) or knockdown shooters (AJ Green, Sam Hauser, Duncan Robinson). Bridges isn't.

Instead, he's only a 34% career 3-point shooter, which complicates his fit next to a non-spacing center. It's worth noting that in 978 minutes together in Charlotte, Bridges and center Mark Williams -- another former Hornet who's now starting in Phoenix's frontcourt -- had a subpar 111.6 offensive rating, per databallr (though the Hornets were generally terrible on offense in those seasons, with Ball so often injured).

One wonders whether the Suns have an overly optimistic view of Bridges because of his connection to Michigan State, where he played for two seasons before entering the NBA draft in 2018. Suns owner Mat Ishbia, coach Jordan Ott and general manager Brian Gregory all spent years at Michigan State; Gregory was a consultant for the program in 2016-17, Bridges' freshman year.

(That might be overstating the case somewhat, as the Suns were rumored to be interested in trading for Bridges as far back as the 2024 trade deadline. That was Bridges' first season after his suspension, and it was before Gregory and Ott joined the organization.)

The Suns also completed this trade with an eye on their cap sheet. Allen and O'Neale will make a combined $29 million in 2026-27 and $31 million in 2027-28 (assuming Allen exercises his player option). Bridges will make $22.8 million in 2026-27 before becoming a free agent next summer; he's eligible to sign an extension worth up to three years and $89 million before then, according to ESPN's Bobby Marks.

That amounts to some savings for the Suns, but only a small amount if they keep Bridges beyond next season -- certainly not enough to warrant the trade of an unprotected first-round pick and the opportunity cost of losing their best trade chip.

The 2029 first-rounder the Suns acquired in exchange -- reacquired, in a way, because they'd first sent Charlotte the rights to the least favorable pick among Utah, Cleveland and Minnesota in the Williams trade -- is much less valuable than an unprotected selection. The Hornets, Jazz, Cavaliers and Timberwolves would all have to miss the playoffs in 2029 for that pick to land in the lottery.

June 26: Pistons add Joe from Thunder for picks
Detroit Pistons get: G Isaiah Joe

Oklahoma City Thunder get: Two second-round picks (2030, 2031)

Grade for Detroit: A-

What this means for the Pistons: Detroit entered the offseason with two glaring weaknesses: secondary creation and shooting, both of which would bolster an offense that was too dependent on Cade Cunningham, without enough support around the All-NBA guard.

Joe won't do much to address the first of those two weaknesses, as he has never averaged more than 1.6 assists per game in a season and is much more of a play finisher than a playmaker.

But he's one of the best options in the league to address the second issue. The Pistons ranked 28th in made 3-pointers last season, with only Duncan Robinson (2.9 per game) and Cunningham (2.0) making more than 1.3 per game.

Joe, meanwhile, made 2.5 triples in just 21 minutes per game. He's a career 41% 3-point shooter, and he has reached that number with impressive consistency. In four seasons in Oklahoma City, his 3-point percentages have been 40.9%, 41.6%, 41.2% and 42.3%.

With an $11.3 million salary for 2026-27, as well as a team option for the same amount in 2027-28, Joe offers that production on a perfectly reasonable contract. His addition could mean the Pistons decide not to keep Robinson -- only $2 million of his $16 million salary is guaranteed -- so they have more financial flexibility to add another star-level scorer, or they could keep both shooters for significantly superior spacing around Cunningham.

Grade for Oklahoma City: B

What this means for the Thunder: Born exactly six months apart, Joe and Aaron Wiggins have a lot in common.

Both were long shots to make an NBA impact: Wiggins was the No. 55 pick in the draft, while Joe was the No. 49 pick before being waived by Philadelphia. But both wings developed into solid rotation players in Oklahoma City, averaging double-digit points in around 20 minutes per game, and both signed extensions that started in 2024-25 and declined over the course of their contracts.

Despite that production and value, both players fell to the fringes of Oklahoma City's postseason rotation, because the Thunder boast the NBA's deepest roster. And ultimately, both players were traded for two second-round picks apiece this summer: Wiggins to Atlanta, Joe to Detroit.

Like the Wiggins trade, the Joe deal is all about the money. Oklahoma City entered the offseason with a projected 2026-27 payroll of $557 million, including both player salaries and luxury tax payments.

But by trading both Wiggins' $9.0 million and Joe's $11.3 million -- and by declining Kenrich Williams' $7.2 million player option -- the Thunder will turn about $27.5 million in salary savings into a whopping $216 million in overall savings, because their tax bill shrinks by $189 million, according to ESPN's Bobby Marks.

The Thunder's updated payroll projection is now $341 million, which is still high, but nowhere near its previous peak. And while they might have cost themselves some regular season wins in the process -- because Wiggins and Joe are high-quality fill-ins when Oklahoma City's regulars miss games -- the elimination of some depth shouldn't move the needle much in the postseason.

At $18 million above the second apron, Oklahoma City might not be done. GM Sam Presti could pursue further transactions to duck below that threshold, such as dealing Luguentz Dort or trading recent draftees Nikola Topic and Thomas Sorber, now that the Thunder picked two more young players at their positions in the 2026 draft.

But if Presti had to cut payroll somehow, then he has done well so far to massage his team's finances while also adding draft capital, rather than having to attach picks to part with undesirable contracts. That's the value of long-term planning.

June 25: Hornets deal Ball to Wolves for Reid, picks
Minnesota Timberwolves get: G LaMelo Ball, F Josh Green

Charlotte Hornets get: F Naz Reid, 2033 unprotected first-round pick, three first-round pick swaps (2028, 2029, 2030), three second-round picks (2029, 2032, 2033)

Grade for Minnesota: D+

What this means for the Timberwolves: The Timberwolves had to make a choice last summer. Julius Randle, Naz Reid and Nickeil Alexander-Walker were potential free agents, and for all intents and purposes, the Western Conference finalists could keep only two. So Minnesota opted for size, re-signing power forwards Randle and Reid and letting the smaller Alexander-Walker leave for Atlanta.

Fast-forward a year, and it's clear the Timberwolves would like a mulligan on that decision: Alexander-Walker is the Most Improved Player winner, while both Randle and Reid are off the team entirely, after two blockbuster trades.

ESPN's Shams Charania reported Monday that Minnesota was sending Randle to Brooklyn in a three-team deal, and that transaction folded in a fourth team Thursday, with an addition that essentially swaps Ball for Reid and future picks.

Minnesota already had little draft capital remaining, as a result of trading for Rudy Gobert and Rob Dillingham in previous summers. The Timberwolves now don't control their own first-round pick in 2027, 2028, 2029, 2030, 2031 or 2033, and their 2032 pick is frozen due to second apron rules.

In other words, this is the last big swing the team can realistically take to build around Anthony Edwards, and to push past the Thunder and Spurs and other Western Conference contenders to actually reach the Finals, rather than stall out a round or two short. Is it enough?

Let's start with a positive frame. Despite the occasional foolish turnover or ill-advised off-balance 3-pointer, Ball is a tremendous offensive engine. He's a solid 3-point shooter on immense volume, an excellent passer and knows how to navigate a pick-and-roll. (He ranked second in the league in total pick volume last season, behind only Jalen Brunson, per GeniusIQ.)

Over the past two seasons, he ranked in the 99th percentile in on/off differential on offense, per Cleaning the Glass, as Charlotte's offense hummed with him on the floor and cratered without him.

According to both estimated plus-minus and xRAPM, which incorporate that on/off data, Ball ranks as one of the five best offensive players in the sport, in terms of per-possession impact. That's a meaningful addition to a team that has lacked playmaking ability ever since veteran point guard Mike Conley began to show his age.

With Edwards and Ball -- the Nos. 1 and 3 picks in the 2020 draft -- Minnesota now boasts one of the NBA's best backcourts. Add in Ayo Dosunmu, who's staying in Minnesota after signing a five-year, $112 million deal, and the Timberwolves have transformed their guard rotation from Edwards and question marks to an undeniable strength.

But now comes the negative side, with two overwhelming concerns. The first is Ball's availability, on which Minnesota is essentially staking its future.

Here are Ball's games played over the past four seasons, since he was an All-Star in Year 2: 36, 22, 47, 72. In that light, last season's 72 games played looks like an outlier -- and even then, the Hornets limited his minutes to just 28 per game to keep him fresh. It's possible Ball has turned the corner and will be healthier going forward, but that's a large gamble.

The second main drawback is what this trade does for Minnesota's roster balance. For as deep and dynamic as the backcourt now looks, the frontcourt appears equally barren, with two of Minnesota's three big men from last season leaving in the same trade.

The Timberwolves' depth chart now features Jaden McDaniels at small forward, Gobert at center and 19-year-old Joan Beringer at backup center -- but a big empty hole where the power forward should be. That's a major issue in a league in which size is once again becoming more important, and it's unclear if the Timberwolves have the resources to address it.

It's possible McDaniels could move up a position, but his greatest strength is his ability to stymie opposing guards. In the playoffs, he most frequently guarded Jamal Murray and De'Aaron Fox, according to GeniusIQ tracking; in the regular season, his most common matchups included bigger wings such as Kevin Durant and Kawhi Leonard, but more lead guards such as Murray, Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and Stephen Curry.

The Timberwolves could also try trading Donte DiVincenzo, who's out indefinitely after tearing his Achilles in the playoffs, for more size. But without attractive draft picks, it could be difficult to incentivize a partner team in that hypothetical deal.

Otherwise, Minnesota has only about $10 million to fill its last three roster spots -- after it signs second-round pick Isaiah Evans -- before reaching the second apron, where it's hard-capped as a result of aggregating players in this trade. That's nowhere near enough room to add the caliber of players it needs to round out a championship-worthy rotation.

For a while now, the Timberwolves have sought to use their scant remaining resources to add star power next to Edwards. And compared to missing on Durant and Giannis Antetokounmpo, Ball seems like a lesser prize. He's still just 24 years old, and if he remains healthy, his contract is fair value for a player with his offensive potential ($130.7 million over the next three seasons, or about 25% of the cap).

But in taking their final big swing on an injury-prone, defensively limited guard who fills one big hole but opens up another just as large, the Timberwolves might have locked themselves into an unwinnable situation. And now they have less flexibility than before, if they want another mulligan next summer.

Grade for Charlotte: B-

What this means for the Hornets: Minnesota isn't the only team breaking up a lineup that worked in the search for something greater: By trading Ball, Charlotte is removing the engine that catalyzed what was by far the NBA's best high-volume lineup last season. In 509 minutes, Ball, Kon Knueppel, Brandon Miller, Miles Bridges and Moussa Diabate outscored their opponents by 26.4 points per 100 possessions, with an eye-popping 134.9 offensive rating.

That lineup surged after the All-Star break, as the Hornets became every NBA nerd's favorite sleeper contender. Charlotte ended up missing the playoffs due to a play-in loss but finished the regular season with the league's eighth-best net rating (plus-4.9) -- two spots better, incidentally, than the Timberwolves.

Now the Hornets are making a significant change, rather than trusting a young group to continue growing together.

Taken on its own, this trade will make the Hornets worse next season, because despite their other exciting young talent, Ball was still their most important player. Their offense scored 123.2 points per 100 possessions with Ball on the court last season, per NBA Advanced Stats. That was better than the Nuggets' league-best rating. But the offense scored just 110.6 points per 100 possessions without Ball, which was equal to the Kings' 26th-ranked unit.

In return, the Hornets primarily gained optionality. Reid is a solid two-way player, if somewhat overpaid with four years and $103.4 million remaining on his contract. Between Reid, No. 14 pick Hannes Steinbach and incumbents Diabate and Ryan Kalkbrenner, the Hornets now boast a fascinating big man rotation, with a blend of skill sets that coach Charles Lee can spend the season exploring.

But the bigger draw for Charlotte is the money and picks involved. In addition to shedding Ball's contract in this deal, the Hornets created a $40.7 million trade exception, which is the largest in NBA history, according to ESPN's Bobby Marks.

They also added an unprotected first-round pick in 2033, which is now their most valuable future draft asset. They hold several other teams' first-round picks in 2027 and 2029, but those have some level of protection.

And while pick swaps have historically been less important than advertised because they don't often convey, they should be more valuable in the new draft system, where every lottery pick is drawn rather than just the top four. (One of the swaps will be a "swap of swaps," however, because Minnesota already owed a swap to a different team in 2030, and the Timberwolves might not even have a pick to swap in 2029, because they owe a top-five-protected pick to Utah.)

Is that future value sufficient to warrant slowing an up-and-coming contender's momentum, after the franchise's most exciting season in more than a decade? That's a trickier case to sell, and it requires trusting the front office: Nobody knows Ball better than the Hornets, so if they're choosing to sell high on the star guard after his healthiest season in years, it's worth wondering whether they know something the Timberwolves don't.

In the meantime, Charlotte can use Knueppel on the ball more, as the rising sophomore continues to develop at the NBA level. They can re-sign free agent Coby White to play on the ball, even if he's underqualified as a lead playmaker. (Editor's note: Shortly after this grade was posted, Charania reported that White intends to sign a three-year, $74 million with the Hornets.) And they can search for a different point guard of the future who's more reliable than Ball, making use of all their extra flexibility to target the right player at the deepest position in the league.

That route limits their potential to continue climbing up the standings next season, but it's a bet that might pay off over the long term.

June 24: Detroit sends Stewart to Memphis
Memphis Grizzlies get: Isaiah Stewart

Detroit Pistons get: Three second-round picks

Grade for Memphis: B+

What this means for the Grizzlies: Spiritually, Stewart might have always been destined to become a Grizzly. Few players in the current NBA embody the "grit 'n' grind" ethos more than the 25-year-old, who has never been afraid to get physical on the court.

In addition to providing that toughness for a fanbase bound to appreciate it, Stewart will serve two key roles for his new team. First, he's an elite rim protector: Stewart allowed opponents to shoot just 44% at the basket last season, per NBA Advanced Stats, which led all players with at least 100 shots defended. The previous season, he ranked second behind Chet Holmgren.

And second, Stewart will provide center insurance behind 7-foot-3 Zach Edey, who pairs immense potential with immense injury risk. Edey played just 11 games last season and has had multiple ankle surgeries in the past 12 months -- an especially worrisome sign for a center of his size.

By the end of last season, with Edey and Santi Aldama injured and Jaren Jackson Jr. traded, the Grizzlies had effectively run out of big men and were playing entire games down the stretch without anyone taller than 6-foot-9.

Stewart himself is only 6-foot-8, but he plays bigger and operates mainly as a center. His 3-point shot has never fully developed (33% last season on 2.1 attempts per game), which makes it difficult for him to play with a non-shooting big. But next to Aldama or No. 3 pick Cameron Boozer -- or even former Utah lottery pick Taylor Hendricks, who showed flashes last season after joining Memphis in the Jackson trade -- Stewart would function as a perfectly competent backup center, or as a fill-in starter when Edey misses time.

Stewart will make $15 million in 2026-27 and has another $15 million via a team option for 2027-28. That eight-figure sum might be too much for Detroit to bear -- more on that below -- but Memphis has plenty of room to absorb Stewart's salary while still retaining flexibility for other moves.

Given that the Grizzlies initially acquired three second-round picks from Detroit during the first round of the draft on Tuesday to move back from the No. 17 pick to No. 21, they effectively added Stewart in exchange for moving back four slots after the lottery. That's good value for a team in their position.

Grade for Detroit: B

What this means for the Pistons: Like with several other moves from contenders this month, the Pistons' motivation to trade Stewart is primarily financial. The salaries for Detroit's young core are growing more expensive: Cade Cunningham is now playing on a max extension, Jalen Duren is a restricted free agent this summer and Ausar Thompson is eligible for an extension.

Trading Stewart's $15 million salary without taking back any money in return bumps Detroit's room below the luxury tax to $75 million, according to ESPN's Bobby Marks. The Pistons could also operate as a cap space team with a few additional maneuvers, such as shedding Duncan Robinson, who has only $2 million of his $16 million salary guaranteed.

So it's almost unfair to give the Pistons a grade for this trade yet, as it's clearly the first domino in a series of moves designed to give the 60-win team a better chance at advancing further than the conference semifinals next season. It remains to be seen how they use their extra wiggle room.

But the Pistons are aiming, above all, for more financial flexibility: to re-sign Duren (who almost has to return at this point, despite his playoff struggles, given that the Pistons traded his backup), re-sign Tobias Harris and add more firepower next to Cunningham.

And while Stewart matched Detroit's ethos just as aptly as he will in Memphis, the Pistons might not miss him as much on the court. Analytics darling Paul Reed is overqualified as a third-string center -- either he or Oklahoma City's Jaylin Williams is the best third-stringer in the league -- and is signed to a nonguaranteed $5.6 million deal for 2026-27. Promoting him to second string would save Detroit nearly $10 million in the tradeoff.

Ultimately, taken on its own, this trade makes the Pistons worse, as they lost a positive contributor without adding anyone in return. But Detroit's front office deserves the benefit of the doubt -- that it has a plan in mind for what more impactful domino should fall next.

June 21: Wolves, Bulls, Nets complete three-way deal
Minnesota Timberwolves get: No. 33 pick (via Nets), Mouhamadou Gueye

Chicago Bulls get: Nic Claxton

Brooklyn Nets get: Julius Randle, No. 28 pick (via Timberwolves)

Grade for Minnesota: B

What this means for the Timberwolves: Two years after they acquired Randle and Donte DiVincenzo in exchange for Karl-Anthony Towns, Towns is an NBA champion while DiVincenzo is out with a torn Achilles and Randle is the subject of a salary dump. If it needed any further clarification, Minnesota definitely lost that blockbuster trade.

But focusing on how the Timberwolves landed Randle two years ago is a matter of the sunk cost fallacy, so let's focus on the present. Minnesota's side of this three-team trade is almost entirely motivated by finances. Randle is owed $33.3 million in 2026-27 and $35.8 million on a player option in 2027-28, as part of an extension he signed last summer.

By trading Randle in a deal involving the two teams with the most cap space in the league, the Timberwolves were able to shed that hefty salary without taking any guaranteed money back in return. They also had to drop just five spots in the draft to do so, even if the difference in "they traded a first-round pick for a second-round pick" overstates that gap.

The Timberwolves' new financial situation places them $42 million below the luxury tax line and $50 million below the first apron. It also gives them access to multiple exceptions they can use to sign players this offseason, as well as a $33.3 million trade exception they could use for a highly paid veteran who fits their roster better.

Step one with all of that extra space was re-signing Ayo Dosunmu, an unrestricted free agent after a positive post-deadline stint with the Timberwolves. Further upgrades are sure to come thereafter, because without Randle or the injured DiVincenzo, the Timberwolves' roster is still very incomplete.

Replacing Randle shouldn't be an insurmountable challenge. His departure opens up a starting slot for sixth man extraordinaire Naz Reid, with whom Rudy Gobert has a proven partnership -- the duo has a plus-9.1 net rating in more than 2,700 minutes together over the past three regular seasons, per databallr.

And while Randle averaged 20 points and 4.9 assists per game over two seasons in Minnesota, his notorious playoff struggles limited his team's upside. For the Timberwolves to make a run at their first Finals berth -- and to get past the Thunder and Spurs in the process -- they couldn't rely on Randle as their No. 2 option behind Anthony Edwards.

But the real problem is what happens once Reid moves to the starting lineup, because the Timberwolves were already relying on a tight playoff rotation, with little depth beyond their top seven or eight players. They'd better make good use of their extra money to round out a more supportive roster, because they're now down two good players from last year's group without adding any suitable replacements -- yet.

Grade for Brooklyn: C+

What this means for the Nets: Welcome back to New York, Julius Randle. The three-time All-Star's first stint in the city, with the Knicks, saw him play alongside a high-scoring veteran forward with trade value (Marcus Morris) and a bunch of young ball handlers (RJ Barrett, Immanuel Quickley, Frank Ntilikina and Dennis Smith Jr., among others), and he looks poised to repeat that experience, with Michael Porter Jr. as the forward with trade value and all of the Nets' 2025 draftees as the young guards.

In a league that no longer rewards tanking as it once did, thanks to new lottery rules, Randle carries extra value as a floor-raiser -- and the Nets, who don't even control their 2027 first-round pick, had might as well try to win some more games next season after losing 50-plus in each of the last three seasons.

In that respect, Randle's greatest ability is his availability. He has played in at least 69 games (or the equivalent in COVID-shortened seasons) in 10 of the past 11 seasons, ranking seventh in total games and eighth in total minutes in that span.

Randle's steady 20 PPG production should boost the Nets' 30th-ranked offense. And while he has never been the most efficient shooter, he's an underrated passer, which could relieve some pressure from the overtaxed group of young guards who struggled last season.

It's fair to wonder, though, what Randle's acquisition amounts to for Brooklyn, which will end up cutting out a major chunk of its cap space this summer to add a player without much value -- at least, on his current contract -- throughout the league. The Nets are still unlikely to be a playoff team next season, barring further meaningful upgrades, and the 31-year-old Randle will likely be well past his prime by the time the Nets are ready to contend.

Moving up five spots in the draft doesn't seem like a large enough difference to justify this trade on an opportunistic basis, either.

The Nets should be more interesting next season as a result of this trade. Randle and Porter form a fascinating forward combination. Day'Ron Sharpe deserves extra playing time, and should slot in as the Nets' starting center with Claxton gone. Multiple first-round picks will join the five first-rounders who already played for Brooklyn last season.

But does this trade make the Nets better, over the long run? It's hard to answer yes with much confidence.

Grade for Chicago: B-

What this means for the Bulls: Trading for Claxton is the first move of new executive vice president of basketball operations Bryson Graham's tenure, and it makes use of the Bulls' copious cap space to add an experienced center essentially for free. (Gueye played two games for Chicago last season, and is on a nonguaranteed deal for 2026-27.)

Claxton has two years left on a contract that declines year over year. He is owed $23.3 million in 2026-27 and $21.1 million in 2027-28, which ranks in the middle of the pack among starting centers. That fits Claxton's status as a middle-of-the-pack center.

Or, at least the Bulls hope he's still at that level. At his best, Claxton's calling card is his defense, but his metrics on that end have declined precipitously over the last few seasons, as he's largely toiled away in obscurity for an out-of-contention Nets squad.

Claxton averaged 2.5 blocks per game in 2022-23, when he received down-ballot Defensive Player of the Year votes. But he's tallied fewer blocks in every season since, down to 1.1 per game last season. At the same time, Claxton has allowed a higher field goal percentage at the rim every year.

Opposing FG% at Rim Against Nicolas Claxton

The Bulls' hope is surely that Claxton felt the effects of not playing an important game for years on end, and that he can reverse his decline in a new environment. (Given the Bulls' rebuild, however, it might be some time before Claxton plays an important game in Chicago, too.)

At 27 years old, Claxton is still theoretically in his prime, and he'll have the runway to grow alongside 21-year-old forward Matas Buzelis and whoever the Bulls select with the No. 4 pick on Tuesday. If North Carolina forward Caleb Wilson lands in Chicago, as ESPN's Jeremy Woo projects, then the Bulls would have a supersized, super-athletic frontcourt for their future -- befitting Graham's "SLAP" philosophy, emphasizing size, length, athleticism and physicality.

"SLAP" applies to Claxton, who has also been one of the NBA's best switching bigs in previous years. But he's a more limited player on the other end: He has never made more than five 3-pointers in a season, and he's a career 56% free throw shooter. He'll enjoy setting screens and rolling to the rim for Josh Giddey lobs, but likely not much else -- though his 3.7 assists per game last season represented a major career high, and hint at untapped playmaking potential.

The larger question about Claxton in Chicago is whether the Bulls would have been better off using their cap space to trade for negative-value contracts and acquire extra draft picks in the process. They are also no longer a threat to offer a large contract to Jalen Duren or Walker Kessler -- two younger, better centers than Claxton -- in restricted free agency.

Claxton might have come essentially for free, in terms of assets, but his arrival still comes with a meaningful opportunity cost.

Still, the Bulls have $31 million in remaining cap space even after adding Claxton, which gives them enough flexibility to take on a bad contract and an associated pick if they desire. And they didn't have any true centers on the roster after they traded Nikola Vucevic last season, so Claxton -- ironically, a polar opposite player stylistically from Vucevic -- fills a massive hole.

Taking on his contract into their cap space means it's fair to treat the Bulls' end of this three-team deal as if they were signing Claxton to a two-year, $44 million contract. That would be decent but not overwhelming value, and their grade here reflects that tradeoff.

June 21: Heat acquire Giannis in massive blockbuster
Miami Heat get: F Giannis Antetokounmpo, F Bobby Portis

Milwaukee Bucks get: G Tyler Herro, C Kel'el Ware, F Jaime Jaquez Jr., G Kasparas Jakučionis , 2026 first-round pick (No. 13), 2031 first-round pick, 2033 first-round pick, 2030 pick swap, 2033 second-round pick

Grade for Miami: B-

What this means for the Heat: The Miami Heat have a reputation as a destination for the stars -- but it has been quite a while since they actually landed one. The last time any Heat player finished higher than 10th in MVP voting was 2013-14, when LeBron James was the runner-up.

Since then, Miami's biggest acquisitions are Jimmy Butler III and lower-level stars such as Goran Dragic, post-prime Kyle Lowry and Terry Rozier (the less said about that transaction, the better). The Heat were routinely in rumors surrounding superstars but didn't turn those hypotheticals into reality.

That inability to close showed on the court. The Heat have reached 50 wins only once in 12 seasons since James left after the 2014 Finals, and they've been stuck in play-in territory four seasons in a row. Two Finals appearances in that span -- including one marvelous run as the No. 8 seed -- helped mask Miami's mediocrity, but this is a team that has been searching for a higher level for a while.

Grade for Milwaukee: B+

What this means for the Bucks: Antetokounmpo's departure closes the book on what is inarguably the greatest individual career in Milwaukee Bucks history. The former No. 15 pick is the franchise's leader in almost every major statistic: games, minutes, points, rebounds, assists, blocks, field goals and free throws. He has 56 triple-doubles for Milwaukee; no other Buck is even in double digits. He's a 10-time All-Star, two-time MVP and one-time Finals MVP, after scoring 50 points to close out the Bucks' first title in 50 years.

But it was long past time for both him and the team to move on. After years of unfortunate injuries (Khris Middleton in 2022), ill-fated transactions (the Damian Lillard trade) and wasted drafts (the last Bucks pick to make a real impact for the team was Donte DiVincenzo, who was drafted eight years ago), the Bucks were no longer a legitimate contender, even with Antetokounmpo still receiving MVP votes.

Over the past four seasons, 15 teams won at least one first-round series. The Bucks weren't one of them.

Read the full grade for the Antetokounmpo trade, plus league winners and losers.

June 21: Hawks acquire G Wiggins from Thunder
Atlanta Hawks get: G Aaron Wiggins

Oklahoma City Thunder get: Two second-round picks (2030, 2032)

Grade for Atlanta: B+

What this means for the Hawks: Wiggins' acquisition continues a solid start to the offseason for Atlanta, which first extended CJ McCollum on a low-risk deal over the weekend. Wiggins also comes with low risk: He's on a good contract -- $9 million in 2026-27, $8.2 million in 2027-28 and $8.2 million on a team option in 2028-29 -- and the Hawks had to surrender only two far-off second-round picks to land him.

In Oklahoma City, Wiggins had fallen to the edges of the NBA's deepest rotation, but he should have a much greater impact in Atlanta. The Hawks have a splendid starting lineup but were frightfully thin by the end of last season; in their six-game playoff loss to New York, Jonathan Kuminga was their only bench player to average more than five points per game or make more than eight total shots all series.

Wiggins can do better than that: He has averaged 17 points per 36 minutes over the past three seasons while making 39% of his 3-pointers. That scoring ability should make him one of the first players off Quin Snyder's bench -- though it does raise further questions about 2024 No. 1 pick Zaccharie Risacher's place in Atlanta's rotation, if Wiggins earns more minutes on the wing.

The only factor dropping Atlanta's grade on this deal from an A to a B+ is uncertainty around Wiggins' true level. His numbers declined across the board in 2025-26 compared to the previous two seasons, most notably a true shooting percentage that was well above league average in 2023-24 (66%) and 2024-25 (60%) but fell below in 2025-26 (54%).

But even middling production would make Wiggins a relatively valuable contributor in Atlanta, given the inferior options he's replacing.

Grade for Oklahoma City: B

What this means for the Thunder: Wiggins is a solid player, but he'd become a luxury in Oklahoma City, where he was the 12th or 13th man in the rotation. While he helped raise the Thunder's floor in the regular season, serving as an effective fill-in when the players ahead of him were injured, he played just 75 minutes in the 2025-26 postseason.

When Wiggins received opportunities to prove he belonged in the Thunder's conference finals clash against San Antonio, the Spurs played him off the floor.

Still, Oklahoma City's decision to trade him is almost entirely motivated by finances, rather than his own play. In addition to removing the $9 million he's owed next season from their books, the Thunder will save a projected $61 million in luxury tax penalties with this trade, according to ESPN's Bobby Marks.

And because Wiggins is on an attractive contract, Thunder GM Sam Presti was able to acquire picks -- even less valuable second-rounders -- while shedding Wiggins' salary, rather than including picks to entice another team to trade for him.

Expect additional moves of this nature as the offseason continues and Oklahoma City seeks to further reduce its exorbitant tax bill, which stands at a projected $152 million.

stories.headline: Columbus Crew 2 fires Higuain after fallout from ref abuse
stories.summary: The Columbus Crew announced that Crew 2 manager Federico Higuain has been fired for cause, effective immediately, in the wake of his suspension by MLS NEXT Pro following an incident of misconduct towards a female referee.
stories.body:
The Columbus Crew announced that Crew 2 manager Federico Higuain has been fired for cause, effective immediately, in the wake of his suspension by MLS NEXT Pro following an incident of misconduct towards a female referee.

"We determined it's in the best interest of our Club, players and support staff to dismiss Federico Higuaín from his responsibilities," said Crew General Manager Issa Tall in prepared statement. "After conversations this week and further assessing the past month, our Club's standards of what's expected from a leader for one of our teams have not been met," The Crew's statement added that for the 2026 MLS NEXT Pro Playoffs, the Crew 2 technical staff will assume additional responsibilities ahead of the Club's search for a full-time head coach for the side.

Higuain, 41, was suspended for two games following an Aug. 23 incident that involved him refusing to let go of the hand of a female referee during the post-game handshake, despite being asked three times to do so. Higuain also directed a sexist remark toward the referee saying: "Don't forget that this is a man's game."

Higuain, who excelled as a player for the Crew over eight seasons, was red carded for the incident. In addition to the two-game suspension, Higuain was ordered to undergo restorative practice training, sources told ESPN.

An MLS NEXT Pro spokesperson confirmed that Higuain was suspended for just one additional game, as the policy allows for the red card to count towards the total suspension. The same spokesperson wasn't able to answer the question of why Higuain's actions didn't constitute a forceful grab.

The Professional Soccer Referees Association (PSRA), the union that represents MLS and USL referees, brought the incident to light over the weekend, stating in a social media post that it was not satisfied with the penalties, adding that a "forceful grab" plus the discriminatory language should have been penalized more severely.

While the PSRA's post didn't mention Higuain by name, ESPN reported that the coach in question was Higuain.

"The League's response falls drastically short of the right message to the participants, the referees, and the public. It needs to be reevaluated," the PSRA's social media post read.

The Crew initially issued a statement stating that, "The Crew actively collaborated with MLS NEXT Pro throughout the review process and fully accepted the additional discipline issued in accordance with league policies.

"We condemn any action or notion that contradicts our mission of uniting and uplifting all communities and genders through the global game."

But sources with knowledge of the Crew's decision to fire its coach told ESPN that the club wasn't satisfied with Higuain's response to the incident, saying there was a "lack of contrition" on his part, that he refused to issue a public apology to the female referee, and that there was an overall lack of accountability on the part of its second-team coach.

There was pressure from several of the Crew's supporters groups as well, including the Nordecke and CapyBrava, which both made social media posts demanding that Higuain be fired.

One source said that Higuain was informed of the club's decision early Tuesday afternoon.

In a statement given to ESPN on Sunday, MLS NEXT Pro said the league "immediately investigated the reported incident between the head coach and the female official. It was determined that the coach's behavior violated League policies and warranted additional discipline beyond the red card that was issued in the moment. He served a two-game suspension and is required to participate in a multi-session restorative practices process, which is already underway. The program is intended to support the League's efforts to foster understanding, accountability, respect, and the restoration of relationships across the League. MLS NEXT Pro believes in the restorative approach. The League is confident in its process and the results."

stories.headline: Ugo Ugochukwu celebrates Nigerian roots after winning FIA Formula 3 championship
stories.summary: Newly crowned FIA Formula 3 champion Ugo Ugochukwu says he is proud to represent his Nigerian heritage on the international stage, even though he races under the United States flag.
stories.body:
Newly crowned FIA Formula 3 champion Ugo Ugochukwu says he is proud to represent his Nigerian heritage on the international stage, even though he races under the United States flag.

Ugochukwu, whose mother is Nigerian supermodel Oluchi Onweagba-Orlandi, became the first American to win the FIA Formula 3 championship after finishing second in the season-ending Feature Race in Madrid earlier this month.

He said during a post-race interview on SuperSport that his Nigerian heritage is a matter of pride: "I think it's amazing. I'm super proud of my Nigerian roots, on my mom's side.

"For me, it makes me very proud every time I can get on the podium, get my name out there to everyone watching and supporting in Africa. That means a lot and hopefully I can be a good role model to all the kids who would like to have this dream as well."

The 19-year-old entered the final weekend 15 points behind Britain's Freddie Slater, but drew level before last Sunday's race after qualifying and Saturday's Sprint Race.

Starting second behind Finland's Tuukka Taponen, Ugochukwu held his position to the finish while Slater came home eighth. The result gave the Campos Racing driver the championship with 159 points, 14 clear of Slater.

"There was a little bit of pressure, which is pretty normal," he said while describing the championship decider. "This last weekend was definitely the most important one of the championship."

With the hard part done in qualifying, the Ugochukwu said his priority in the final race was to protect the position he needed to secure the title, instead of chasing Taponen for the victory and putting it all at risk.

"We knew that was what I needed to win the championship, so it was just about getting it home," he said.

The championship win has attracted even more attention in Nigeria, where his maternal heritage means that Nigerians have followed his progress through the international racing ranks, all the way from his go-carting beginnings.

Born in New York to Onweagba-Orlandi and Italian fashion designer Luca Orlandi, Ugochukwu represents the United States in international competition. His mother won the inaugural M-Net Face of Africa competition in 1998 before going on to an international modelling career that included work with some of the world's leading fashion houses.

This Nigerian connection has previously brought public recognition from prominent Nigerians. After he won the Macau Grand Prix in 2024, Nigerians in Diaspora Commission Chair Abike Dabiri-Erewa congratulated him, while former presidential candidate Peter Obi also celebrated the achievement, pointing to his Nigerian heritage.

That Macau victory made Ugochukwu the first American to win the event since Bob Earl in 1981 and added to a record that already included the 2020 FIA Karting European Championship junior title and the inaugural Euro 4 Championship in 2023.

He added the Formula Regional Oceania championship earlier this year before returning for his second season in Formula 3.

His first F3 campaign with PREMA Racing in 2025 produced two podium finishes and 16th place in the championship. Now, the move to Campos Racing for 2026 has brought an immediate improvement, beginning with victory in the opening Feature Race in Melbourne.

Ugochukwu also won the Sprint Race at Silverstone and finished the season with two victories and seven podiums on his way to the title.

"This was the main goal at the start of the year, to get the championship," he said after Sunday's race. "I think after quali we knew we did our job, we did the main task, and today, and yesterday, it was just about execution and getting the points and bringing it home."

The title also drew congratulations from seven-time Formula One champion Lewis Hamilton, who visited with the young champ and acknowledged his achievement on Instagram.

Ugochukwu was part of McLaren's driver development program from the age of 13, when the Formula One team signed him to a long-term agreement following his success in karting.

The FIA Formula 3 Championship, which sits immediately below Formula 2, is on the principal development ladder to Formula One, with recent champions Oscar Piastri and Gabriel Bortoleto among those who subsequently progressed to F1.

stories.headline: Still at zero: Viral Man United fan's haircut challenge nears two years
stories.summary: Viral Manchester United fan Frank Ilett's haircut challenge is nearing the two-year mark and he's back to square 1.
stories.body:
For most clubs, failure or success can be defined in points, trophies and medals. Manchester United are the same, but they can also define it in days. More specifically, it can be summed up in 712 days.

That's how long viral United fan Frank Ilett, also known as The United Strand, has gone without a haircut as he waits for the team to win five games in a row.

After finishing last season with wins over Nottingham Forest and Brighton, Michael Carrick's side could have completed the job with wins over newly promoted Hull City and Ipswich Town before finishing with a win away at Everton. As it turned out, that's not at all what happened.

An embarrassing 2-0 away defeat to Hull meant going back to square one. A 5-2 win over Ipswich might have promoted hopes that the season opener was just an unwanted blip, but a draw to Everton and a controversial defeat to 10-man Manchester City poured further cold water.

How could it get worse? Well, a 2-0 lead inside the first 10 minutes against Brighton in the Carabao Cup ended in a surprise 3-2 defeat.

Left watching on, his hair growing ever longer, is Ilett. His challenge will now officially reach the two-year mark -- his last haircut was on Oct. 5, 2024 -- and his hair is now almost 14 inches at its longest point.

In the meantime, Ilett continues to raise money for the Little Princess Trust, which creates wigs for children with cancer.

The only thing that can happen now before Ilett soars past two years is for United to win away to Fulham in their last game before the international break.

Cleary has been the focus ever since, as first he avoided suspension for a dangerous contact charge, and then set about rehabilitating an injured foot. The Panthers have proven they can win games without Cleary, but his coolness under pressure is invaluable in the biggest games.

The Knights are playing with the casino's money at this stage. After finishing last in 2025, making the finals surpassed anyone's expectations. They simply have to keep playing the way they have been playing. Fast moving defence, free flowing ball movement from anywhere on the field, and total belief in their ability to beat anyone. Without Jacob Saifiti, they are a little light on up front, but veteran Tyson Frizell has stepped up in the middle and the Knights back-row ranks, strengthened now by the surprise return of Dylan Lucas, have been simply brilliant.

The big question is; can the Knights execute their attacking style against the best defence in the business? They played just the once this season, with the Panthers winning 44-12. We know how good the Panthers are. We have seen them dominate the big games for years. Cleary and Dylan Edwards orchestrating the attack, Isaah Yeo and Liam Martin leading the defence. stories.headline: Lowe's sacrifice fly breaks tie and lifts Guardians past Red Sox, 3-2, helping them atop AL Central
stories.summary: — Nathaniel Lowe had a tiebreaking sacrifice fly off reliever Erik Miller in the ninth inning, and the Cleveland Guardians maintained their slim first-place lead in the AL Central with a 3-2 victory over the Boston Red Sox on Tuesday night.
stories.body:
BOSTON -- — Nathaniel Lowe had a tiebreaking sacrifice fly off reliever Erik Miller in the ninth inning, and the Cleveland Guardians maintained their slim first-place lead in the AL Central with a 3-2 victory over the Boston Red Sox on Tuesday night.


Angel Martínez had three hits for the Guardians, who entered the day with a one-game lead over the White Sox atop the Central. Chicago owns the tiebreaker by winning the season series. Cleveland stranded 15 baserunners.


The loss was Boston’s eighth in 12 games, spoiling Chad Tracy’s first game as manager after the club named him its 49th in team history.


Adley Rutschman added three hits for Boston, which clinched one of the AL’s wild-card spots Sunday.


Boston pinch hitter Mickey Gasper hit Hunter Gaddis’ first pitch, tying it at 2-2 leading off the eighth.


Gaddis (5-3) got the win and Cade Smith the final three outs for his 40th save.


Miller (4-2) hit a batter and gave up two hits in an inning.


A strong candidate for the AL Rookie of the Year, Cleveland left-hander Parker Messick gave up a run over five innings. He lowered his ERA to 2.55 and is on pace to become the fourth rookie starting pitcher in MLB history with an ERA under 2.60 and averaging 9.0 or more strikeouts per nine innings.


In his tune-up for a likely playoff start next week, Boston lefty Payton Tolle struggled with his control over 5 2/3 innings, giving up two runs on eight hits. In his previous start on Sept. 13, he had Boston’s second recorded immaculate inning that opened a game.


Up next

stories.headline: Rest-of-season rankings: Walker, Shough on the rise while Maye, McConkey fall
stories.summary: Need a quick free agent pickup -- or roster overhaul -- after Week 2? These rankings are designed to help.
stories.body:
Each week, Eric Karabell ranks players by position based on their fantasy football value for the rest of the 2026 season. Use the information to optimize the players for their future potential and/or to gauge their value in trade. Eric's top 100 can be found below the positions in this column.

Quarterback

Rankings changes: Wow. Serious injuries to the top two selections from the 2024 draft and a late 2025 first-rounder are the story, as fantasy managers will miss the Bears' Caleb Williams (hamstring), Commanders' Jayden Daniels (elbow) and Giants' Jaxson Dart (knee) for an undetermined length of time. Each was among our top 10 QBs. Perhaps the mercurial Williams will return far sooner, so he remains in QB2 range in these rankings, but the risk of reinjury is high. Dart might be lost for the season. Backups Jameis Winston and Marcus Mariota enter the rankings, and they might be playing for months.

With three passers dropping in the rankings, nearly everyone else rises. The 49ers' Brock Purdy, Chiefs' Patrick Mahomes, Saints' Tyler Shough and Lions' Jared Goff are all in the top 10. The Panthers' Bryce Young rises into safer QB2 territory, with room for more. The Patriots' Drake Maye, last year's No. 2 QB scorer, remains in the top 10, but perhaps not for long after two disappointing outings totaling 17.84 points. The Rams' Matthew Stafford rebounds from Australia and is No. 11. It is quite amazing how quickly fantasy value changes in the NFL.

Running back

Rankings changes: Volume is king, and no running back earned more in Week 2 than the Chiefs' Kenneth Walker III. Will he stay healthy? That was an offseason concern, but so far he looks awesome and he continues rising into the top 10. For those who want Walker at No. 1 ... c'mon, we are not there yet. Walker versus Bijan Robinson? It feels premature, though Robinson does drop a spot behind Jonathan Taylor to No. 3. Praise Walker, but if a Robinson investor offers him for Walker, do it.

Broncos rookie Jonah Coleman is among the big risers at running back, though we lack confirmation of solid volume moving ahead (same with the Patriots' TreVeyon Henderson). The Buccaneers' Bucky Irving and Panthers' Chuba Hubbard rise to RB2 status, as their reported timeshares appear to be rather one-sided. Aaron Jones Sr. is healthy and seeing volume. Don't forget about the Saints' Alvin Kamara and Seahawks' Zach Charbonnet, and watch for injury updates on the Eagles' Saquon Barkley.

Wide receiver

Rankings changes: Many star receivers delivered in Week 2, but the rankings movement at this position happened in the late WR2 range, as the Panthers' Jalen Coker, Packers' Christian Watson, Broncos' Jaylen Waddle, Jaguars' Parker Washington and Browns' Denzel Boston continue to add value. Perhaps they catch some early underachievers such as the Falcons' Drake London and Cowboys' George Pickens soon. They have already passed the Chargers' Ladd McConkey and Lions' Jameson Williams.

Tight end

Rankings changes: It might be panic time for investors of several top tight ends, as the Raiders' Brock Bowers has yet to play, and the Bears' Colston Loveland isn't even averaging one fantasy point! (He has one reception for three yards). Try to be patient. We move the Chiefs' Travis Kelce, Bills' Dalton Kincaid and Texans' Dalton Schultz up. The Panthers' Darren Waller is interesting, and the Chargers' Oronde Gadsden might be too. The Falcons' Kyle Pitts Sr. has disappointed us again. Zach Ertz is again an Eagle, but potential investors must keep initial expectations in check.

stories.headline: 'It's pretty cool': Cox reveals what a premiership would mean for Fremantle
stories.summary: Mason Cox says Fremantle's bid for its first premiership is less about what it would mean for him and more about giving the club's long-suffering supporters a memory they can cherish forever.
stories.body:
Fremantle ruck Mason Cox says Fremantle's bid for its first premiership is less about what it would mean for him and more about giving the club's long-suffering supporters a memory they can cherish forever.

The Dockers will face Brisbane in Saturday's Grand Final with the chance to deliver the first flag in the club's history, and Cox says the opportunity is one he feels privileged to be part of.

"It's not as much about what it means to me, it's probably more about the Fremantle community," Cox said on ESPN's Red Time podcast.

"I feel like they've kind of been trotted on over the years. There's a lot of people who have supported the club through thick and thin that have a lot of faith and hope in this team, and are really excited for the opportunity that's ahead.

"As players, you just wanna provide that hope, and hopefully provide that success for them, and give them a great memory."

Cox is one of just three Fremantle players with previous Grand Final experience, having played in Collingwood's 2018 loss to West Coast before helping the Magpies beat Brisbane in the 2023 decider. The 35-year-old said that experience has brought added responsibility to this week.

"You probably share a few more stories from your past experiences, try and keep everybody as calm as possible because there is a lot going on," Cox said.

"I've seen every single side of it. So being able to share that with the players I think is valuable."

Fremantle enters the decider having won just three of its 12 quarters across its three finals -- a loss to Hawthorn before wins over Geelong and Sydney. But Cox said the Dockers were more focused on the detail behind those numbers rather than the headlines.

"You look at that, and some of the stats and everything else, it's proof that this team could be very damaging for a very long time. We're still learning week on week, and we're still trying to get better week on week," he said.

"You look at some of the headlines of three out of 12 quarters and it's like, yeah, people will talk about that whatever, but for us we go into finer detail as to what can actually help us as a team be more successful."

Cox also expects Brisbane to bring an attacking threat, with the Lions having produced big scores in recent weeks -- 133 against Hawthorn following putting 144 on the board against the Crows in the semifinal -- and it's something he insists his side are planning for.

For Cox, though, the prospect of helping Fremantle end its premiership drought remains the biggest motivation of all.

"To be in a situation where the club's trying to win their first flag ever, it's pretty cool and it's very unique," he said.

"That's what sport's all about."
